State of the art (2024-2026): Socratic LLM tutoring has moved from single-prompt 'don't give the answer' chatbots to explicit pedagogical architectures. Consensus points:

(1) Base LLMs default to answering, and scale does not fix it. In HeuristicEdu (arXiv 2607.22996) an unaligned Qwen-72B scored 0% scaffolding effectiveness with 96.7% keyword leakage. SafeTutors (2603.17373) shows multi-turn failures rising from 17.7% to 77.8%, and Tio et al. (2606.11744) show frontier models fail at long sessions. MathTutorBench (2502.18940, EMNLP'25) finds subject expertise does not translate into good teaching, and longer dialogs are harder.

(2) Withholding answers matters causally. Bastani et al. (PNAS 2025) found that unguarded GPT-4 cut later unassisted grades by 17%, while the Socratic 'GPT Tutor' mitigated this. Brender et al. (2607.03303, AIED'26 best paper) found Socratic guidance gave higher later learning gains than prompt-refinement tutoring. The LearnLM/Eedi RCT (2512.23633) reported 66.2% vs 60.7% success on novel problems, with tutors praising LearnLM's Socratic questions.

(3) Pedagogy is being moved out of one prompt into explicit structure. Examples: a curriculum or prerequisite graph with a sequencing policy (Tio), a transition graph of tutoring states (StratL 2410.03781), state-space planning with a learner knowledge state (TreeInstruct 2406.11709), a deterministic help-ceiling ladder with an LLM judge and a deterministic leak detector (Pisan 2608.12292), a Dean critic over the Teacher (SocraticLM, NeurIPS'24), and mastery-graph gating between instructing and solving against 'pedagogical jailbreaks' (SHAPE 2604.22134, ACL'26). Kestin et al. (Sci Rep 2025) state directly that a system prompt could not reliably sequence multi-part scaffolding, so the platform had to.

(4) Turn-level recipes converge on the same loop: perceive the learner state, choose a move, elicit one reflective question. Sources: GuideEval (2508.06583); SocraticLM's four response classes (irrelevant, question, incorrect, correct); MathDial's moves (Focus, Probing, Telling, Generic); Paul-Elder question types (SocratiQ); misconception-to-contradiction trajectories, an operational elenchus (2511.00371); and SocraticMATH's review, guidance, rectification, summarization structure (2407.17349).

(5) Training routes exist but need model weights. They include RL with simulated students (2505.15607; PEARL 2605.29582; HeuristicEdu), DPO (Scarlatos et al. 2503.06424; Kumar & Lan 2403.00199; Petukhova et al. 2606.21502) and representation alignment against 'scaffolding collapse' (2607.19371). For an API-only GigaChat demo, the practical translation is:
- use their reward components (pedagogical quality, leakage, learner correctness) as the critic/judge rubric;
- use their simulated-student methodology for offline evaluation.
StudentSim (2609.01591) cautions that LLM role-play students do not reliably match real competence.

Open debates:
- How strict to be. Eastwood et al. (2609.29995) found the context-aware Socratic assistant rated least supportive. CoMeT (2609.22993) shows contingent escalate/fade reduces frustration compared with question-only tutoring. Deffarges et al. (2609.00584) found Socratic-mode users progressively disengaged, and unrestricted chat won on immediate post-tests. Feng et al. (2607.01692) found students resist Socratic dialogue under time pressure.
- Benchmarks vs reality. Neagu et al. (2606.15766) show real students often do not take up the scaffolding.
- Adaptivity. ExplainRoute (2609.03470) found no reliable advantage of adaptive routing over fixed strategies.
- Reliability of LLM judges.

Design implication for the OKR/GigaChat pipeline:
- A Python orchestrator holds an OKR concept graph and a stage machine (activate, attempt, probe misconceptions, consolidate, transfer, reflect) plus a learner-state model.
- Each turn: classify the learner reply, update mastery, pick a move, question type and hint ceiling, then generate with GigaChat under a hidden contract that includes a reference answer key and a hidden plan.
- A second 'Dean' pass checks the draft against a collapse checklist before display.
- Tone is empathic and growth-mindset, with contingent escalation and fading.
- The session ends with an unassisted transfer check, and the pipeline is evaluated with scripted adversarial and struggling personas over full multi-turn dialogues.

STATE OF THE ART (2023 to Sep 2026). The field has moved from "prompt an LLM to be Socratic" to an explicit pedagogical policy layer placed between understanding the learner and generating text. Three convergent lines of evidence support this.

(1) Decide first, then generate.
- Bridge (2310.10648): conditioning GPT-4 on an expert's decision triple (error, strategy, intention) raised preference by 76%, and random decisions cut quality by 97%.
- Strategize-before-teaching (2302.13496, EACL Findings 2023): predicting the strategy first, then generating, beats generating directly.
- StratL (2410.03781): an LLM classifies the student's state, a deterministic, expert-authored transition graph picks the next tutoring intents, and the LLM only verbalises them.
- SLOW (2603.28062, AIED 2026): separating learner-state inference (cognitive plus affective) from action selection improves personalisation and emotional sensitivity.
- TACT (2608.03952): a 13-strategy tutor taxonomy plus a student-move taxonomy, with SFT and GRPO on top.
- Why this is the consensus: LLMs struggle to predict good tutor strategy themselves (2507.06910, BEA 2025), and a system prompt alone does not hold structure over many turns (Kestin et al., Sci Rep 2025: the tutor went out of sequence, so the platform had to sequence the steps).

(2) Help must be graduated and contingent. This is the classic AutoTutor cycle (pump -> hint -> prompt -> assertion, then restate), reborn as typed help ladders:
- Pisan (2608.12292): an eight-rung ladder whose ceiling is computed by non-LLM code from trusted learner state, plus a deterministic filter and an LLM judge.
- CoMeT (2609.22993): escalate one rung on failure at a decision point and fade to the lightest rung on take-up. This matched a pure question-only tutor's metacognitive demand, frustrated learners less, and leaked the full answer far less often (1/16 vs 1/6 sessions).
- Field evidence that withholding matters: Bastani et al. (PNAS 2025) found unguarded GPT-4 reduced later exam scores by 17%, while a hint-only tutor grounded in teacher-provided solutions and mistakes avoided that. Tutor CoPilot (2410.03017) showed that expert-model guidance increased guiding questions and reduced answer-giving in a 1,800-student RCT (+4 p.p. mastery).
- Authentic usage shows the default problem: over 95% of LLM responses in a university course were at the 'Explaining' or 'Solving' level (2608.22993).

(3) The tutor must balance competing objectives. Pedagogy (no leakage, scaffolding) trades off against learner success and helpfulness:
- RL work makes the trade-off explicit as a Pareto frontier: 2505.15607 (EMNLP 2025), 2503.06424 (AIED 2025), and PEARL (2605.29582) with a controllable student simulator and a multi-objective reward. So do the DPO methods (2402.05000, 2606.21502).
- MathTutorBench (2502.18940) finds that subject expertise does not translate into teaching, and that simple questioning strategies fail in longer dialogues.
- Crucially for an API-only GigaChat build, training-free prompt optimisation matched or beat the strongest RL baseline on all 12 methods tested (2605.27088). LearnLM (2412.16429) frames pedagogy as instruction following of system-level pedagogy specifications. Together these justify a hidden-prompt plus external-policy design with no fine-tuning.

OPEN DEBATES AND RISKS
- Who chooses the move. StratL argues expert-authored graphs are more faithful than letting the LLM choose (as in Bridge). Learned or steerable policies are emerging: PIVOT activation steering (2608.07509), and latent-state RL over high-level actions (2507.16252).
- Over-scaffolding. Pure Socratic questioning frustrates learners (CoMeT). Real students often bypass scaffolding in pursuit of their own goals (2606.15766), and 'learners often did not answer'. Non-uptake must be a handled state, not an error.
- Robustness. Pedagogical jailbreaks and adversarial answer-seeking break prompt-only tutors (SHAPE 2604.22134, ACL 2026; answer-leakage benchmark 2604.18660, ACL 2026). Both motivate gating and verification outside the prompt.
- Evaluation validity. Simulated students built by prompting are poor proxies (2601.04025, ACL 2026). General 'helpfulness' LLM-judge scores do not track pedagogy (2607.28128); rubric judges should be paired with deterministic process measures (leakage, independent-work rate). RL on proxy rewards can reward-hack (2604.04237).

DESIGN IMPLICATIONS FOR THE OKR/GigaChat PIPELINE
- Represent the OKR text as expectations plus known misconceptions (AutoTutor EMT), grouped into decision points (CoMeT).
- Per turn:
  (a) An LLM state tracker outputs JSON: expectation coverage, misconception, affect, uptake/non-answer, attempts per decision point.
  (b) A deterministic Python policy (StratL-style transition graph over lesson phases) picks one tutor move from a PIVOT/MathDial-style taxonomy (pump, focus, hint, prompt, revoice-and-press, contrast example, assertion, metacognitive reflection) and a hint-ladder ceiling (Pisan).
  (c) GigaChat generates N candidates from a hidden LearnLM-style pedagogy prompt plus the per-turn intent.
  (d) A judge enforces the rung ceiling, move compliance, and empathy/revoicing features (2512.20780), and selects the best candidate (2503.06424 applied at inference).
  (e) After any bottom-out explanation, the tutor requires a restatement, and the lesson ends with an unaided transfer task (Bastani).
- Validate with scripted adversarial and misconception personas, and report a Pareto view of leakage vs. learner success (2505.15607, 2605.27088).

State of the art (2024-2026): AI-tutor evaluation has converged on the multi-dimensional pedagogical taxonomy of Maurya et al. (NAACL 2025, MRBench): mistake identification, mistake location, not revealing the answer, guidance, actionability, coherence, tone and human-likeness. The BEA 2025 shared task operationalised it, and MathTutorBench (EMNLP 2025) extended it with a trained pedagogical reward model and long-dialogue variants. Google's LearnLM line adds a principle-level rubric: manage cognitive load, inspire active learning, deepen metacognition, stimulate curiosity, adapt to the learner. The Jurenka et al. 2024 evaluation-driven report (arXiv 2407.12687) founded this line, and it was used in a blind multi-turn expert arena and backed by an RCT showing LLM tutoring matched or beat human tutors on transfer (+5.5 pp). The newest Socratic-specific work (GuideEval) evaluates adaptive guidance as Perception, then Orchestration, then Elicitation rather than question generation alone.

Consensus: (1) Pedagogy and subject expertise are different capabilities. Strong solvers reveal answers (GPT-4 in about 47% of MRBench responses). (2) Quality degrades over multi-turn dialogue: SafeTutors reports failures rising from 17.7% to 77.8%, MathTutorBench finds simple questioning fails later in dialogues, and 'scaffolding collapse' under student pressure (arXiv 2607.19371) shows the same. Evaluation must therefore be multi-turn. (3) Answer withholding cannot be secured by a prompt alone. Robust systems add a deterministic policy layer (a help ladder) plus a separate judge/critic pass (Pisan 2026), and are red-teamed with adversarial or disengaged learner personas (Zhao et al. ACL 2026; DAS2).

Open debates: (a) LLM-as-judge reliability. Off-the-shelf judges correlated negatively with humans on MRBench, the best BEA systems reach only about 0.58-0.72 macro-F1, and 'helpfulness' rubrics are judge-contingent and blind to pedagogy (Fan et al. 2026). The recommended fix is pedagogy-specific, sample-specific rubrics (TutorBench) plus deterministic process metrics (answer leakage, the learner's independent work, uptake) and human calibration. (b) Simulated-student validity. Prompted simulators are weak (Scarlatos et al. ACL 2026) and sycophantically drop their misconceptions after any correction (near-zero Selective Flip Score). MathDial (EMNLP Findings 2023) pioneered LLM students with scripted misconceptions, and fidelity is still the bottleneck. (c) Rigid scaffolding versus learner agency: real students often bypass scaffolding (Neagu et al. 2026), so tutors should negotiate goals and adapt rather than enforce questioning. (d) Empathy: expert-like quality correlates with revoicing and pressing for reasoning, not with extra politeness (Abdulsalam and Aroyehun).

Implications for the GigaChat OKR pipeline: use the Maurya dimensions and the LearnLM principles as the hidden-prompt spec and as the evaluation rubric. Add a per-turn learner-state classifier and strategy selector, a help-ladder policy and a critic pass that checks each draft (no answer, one question, actionable). Run an evaluation harness with persona simulators (engaged, faithful misconception, answer-seeker/adversarial, wheel-spinning, off-task), deterministic metrics (leakage rate, question-ending rate, learner word share, uptake) and a calibrated LLM judge with OKR-specific rubrics. End each session with a transfer task to measure mastery.

State of the foundations (what a Socratic LLM tutor should inherit):
1) Classical structure. The Socratic method combines elenchus (cross-examining the learner's own definition until it clashes with their other commitments), aporia (the resulting productive impasse) and maieutics (the tutor, 'barren' of answers, helps the learner produce and then test their own idea). Vlastos's 'problem of the elenchus' matters for design: refutation shows inconsistency, not truth. So a tutoring pipeline must add the constructive step that ancient dialogues often skip: consolidation after aporia. D'Mello et al. (2014) give the empirical version: induced confusion helps only when it is tied to the content and then resolved.
2) Question inventory. The Paul and Elder taxonomy (clarification, assumptions, reasons/evidence, implications, viewpoints; operationalised in SocratiQ, EACL 2023) is the standard move set for choosing and auditing Socratic questions.
3) Dialogue skeleton. AutoTutor's EMT framework (Nye, Graesser & Hu 2014) is the best-validated operational model, with gains of about 0.8 sigma over reading. It works as follows: a deep main question, a hidden list of expectations and misconceptions, a graduated pump, hint, prompt, assertion ladder, corrections and a summary, inside a 5-step frame where 'do you understand?' is replaced by a knowledge check. LLM-era systems reuse exactly this skeleton. Ruffle&Riley induces the EMT script from a lesson text, which is the closest analogue to the OKR task. MWPTutor has the LLM fill a finite-state transducer. StratL steers the LLM with a transition graph of per-turn tutoring intents.
4) Why prompting beats telling. Chi et al. (2001) found that tutors forbidden to explain and only prompting produced equal learning. ICAP (Chi & Wylie 2014) says learning rises from Passive to Interactive, and a dialogue is interactive only if both sides contribute constructively and the tutor does not dominate. Self-explanation prompts (g = 0.55) and retrieval practice (Roediger & Karpicke 2006: testing beats restudying at a delay, while restudying inflates confidence) give the concrete learner activities. Productive failure (Sinha & Kapur 2021: g = 0.36, 0.87 bias-corrected) supports 'attempt first, then consolidate' for adults on conceptual content.
5) Effect-size realism. Bloom's 2 sigma (tutoring plus mastery checks) is aspirational. VanLehn (2011) finds human tutoring d = 0.79 and ITS d = 0.76, and argues that interaction granularity finer than the step level adds little (the interaction plateau). Recent LLM evidence: Kestin et al. (2025 RCT) report 0.73-1.3 SD over in-class active learning with a research-based prompt, pre-written solutions, and sequencing enforced outside the LLM. Bastani et al. (PNAS 2025) show unguarded GPT-4 access harmed later unassisted performance by 17%, while a guarded tutor mitigated the harm.

Consensus for pipeline design:
- Keep pedagogy in an explicit controller (state machine or intent graph, plus per-expectation learner model) and use the LLM to verbalise moves and grade answers. Prompts alone drift, leak answers and cannot sequence reliably (Kestin; StratL; MWPTutor).
- Ground every turn in the lesson text and a hidden answer key.
- Grade expectation coverage strictly, because Ruffle&Riley's LLM was lenient on partial answers and skipped expectations.
- Measure learning with delayed or unassisted deep items, not in-dialogue success or satisfaction. Ruffle&Riley improved perceived understanding but not test scores.
- Make empathy adaptive. Supportive moves that attribute difficulty to the material help low-knowledge learners but can hurt high-knowledge ones.

Open debates:
- How much of the benefit is Socratic questioning itself versus structure and retrieval (Ruffle&Riley showed no significant gain over reading).
- The optimal amount of interactivity: the interaction plateau, and 'dosage' results showing mixed intense and no dialogue beat constant dialogue.
- Boundary conditions of productive failure: it reverses for young learners and domain-general skills.
- Robustness of answer-withholding under learner pressure. Recent 2026 preprints on 'scaffolding collapse' (2607.19371) and supervisor-based withholding (2608.12292) show this is still unsolved by prompting alone.
- Whether LLM judges can reliably assess free-text explanations.

State of the art (2024-2026): affect is now treated as a first-class signal in LLM tutoring, but the evidence says empathy must be calibrated and subordinate to the epistemic goal.

(1) Productive confusion is the core mechanism a Socratic tutor exploits. Classic work (D'Mello & Graesser 2012; D'Mello et al. 2014) shows that confusion from cognitive conflict improves posttest and transfer performance only if it is resolved. Unresolved confusion turns into frustration and then boredom. A Socratic pipeline should therefore deliberately induce conflict (a flawed OKR, conflicting opinions) and also monitor for the confusion-to-frustration transition.

(2) Affect can be read from text by LLMs themselves. Zero-shot LLM ensembles give usable affect trajectories on about 17k tutoring turns (Zhang et al. 2025). LLM-labelled student state agreed with human labels at kappa = .74 on StudyChat (Abrar et al. 2026, arXiv:2607.09919); the same study found verification feedback had the highest productive-continuation rate and direct answers the lowest. States are short-lived, so they must be re-estimated every turn.

(3) Empathy helps less than expected on its own. LLMs are already perceived as highly empathetic: in Chowdhury et al. (BEA 2025, arXiv:2506.08702), 80% of teacher-annotators preferred the LLM tutor over human tutors on empathy. But in naturalistic logs, empathetic language is not associated with resolving confusion, whereas concrete elaboration is, and long answers hurt (Sharmin et al. 2026). An LLM emotional-support layer improved efficiency and perceived caring but not learning (Rief et al. 2026). Affect-sensitivity helps most for low-knowledge learners (Affective AutoTutor).

(4) The main risk is sycophancy. Warmth training raises error rates by 10-30 pp and makes models validate false beliefs, especially from sad users (Ibrahim et al., Nature 2026). Tutors retreat under authority and face-saving pressure (Kasneci & Kasneci 2026), a learner's wrong answer drags LLM correctness down by up to 15 pp (Arvin 2025), and praise inflation is its own failure mode, strongest in interpretive domains such as business concepts (Vennemeyer et al. 2026).

The emerging consensus is 'kind but correct' ('social-epistemic courage'): politeness and face-saving in form (Wang et al. 2008 politeness effect), with no compromise in content. Person, Kreuz, Zwaan & Graesser (Cognition and Instruction, 1995) showed that human tutors' politeness norms themselves can inhibit effective negative feedback, which is the human analogue of LLM sycophancy.

(5) Motivation and agency. Praise should be specific and process- or strategy-focused, never about traits (Mueller & Dweck 1998), and growth-mindset-supportive language can be produced reliably by LLMs (Handa et al. 2023). Unguarded answer-giving harms later unaided performance by 17% (Bastani et al., PNAS 2025). Pure question-only Socratic tutoring frustrates learners, while contingent escalate-and-fade scaffolding keeps metacognitive demand with less frustration (Hou et al. 2026). Metacognitive feedback rather than rewards reduces offloading (Maier et al. 2026). Real students often bypass scaffolding to pursue their own goals (Neagu et al. 2026, arXiv:2606.15766), so the tutor should negotiate and offer choices rather than rigidly impose a script.

Open debates:
- How much, and what kind, of empathy actually improves learning, beyond perceived care.
- Reliability of text-only affect detection; much of the evidence is correlational or LLM-labelled.
- Multi-turn sycophancy measurement and judge reliability.
- Where to draw the line between productive struggle and harmful frustration.
- Cultural calibration of politeness and directness (relevant for Russian-speaking learners; no direct evidence found).

Design implication for the OKR/GigaChat pipeline:
- Run a hidden per-turn 'state tracker' call covering knowledge per OKR criterion, affect (engaged / productive confusion / frustration / boredom / anxiety), answer-seeking and overconfidence.
- Feed that state to a policy that picks the Socratic move from a contingent hint ladder.
- Generate the reply under hidden constraints: at most one brief empathic clause, one concrete example when confused, one question per turn, process-specific praise only when a rubric criterion is met, and a correctness verdict that is invariant to social pressure.
- Evaluate against a small red-team set of pressured and emotional learner turns.

State of the art (2024-2026): learner modelling inside open-ended tutoring dialogue has become its own research line.

(1) Dialogue knowledge tracing (Scarlatos et al., LAK'25; Huang et al., 2026) uses an LLM to label each student turn with KCs and correctness, then traces mastery turn by turn. Classic KT (BKT/DKT) is near chance on dialogue data. Text-aware LLMKT is clearly better, and IRT-style difficulty modelling adds interpretability. TRAVER (ACL Findings'25) shows that an explicit per-KC textual belief updated every turn, plus a turn-level verifier, raises tutoring success; ablating KT or the verifier hurts. A clear consensus is to separate what the learner knows (a state) from what to say (generation).

(2) Perception before generation. GuideEval (2025) formalises Socratic guidance as Perception → Orchestration → Elicitation. It finds that frontier LLMs answer confused, wrong and correct learners almost identically, and it names indiscriminate affirmation as a key failure. Stepwise verification (Daheim et al.) and generate-retrieve-rerank misconception diagnosis (Mitton et al., L@S'26) show that an explicit diagnosis step grounds replies and cuts hallucination. The classic AutoTutor EMT dialogue (Graesser, IJAIED 2016) is still the cleanest operational template: anticipated expectations and misconceptions, semantic matching, and a pump→hint→prompt→assertion ladder until all expectations are covered, with reported gains of about 0.3-0.8 sigma. Al-Hossami & Bunescu (2025) turn the Socratic elenchus into a computable object: a reasoning trajectory from a misconception to a contradiction and then a belief update.

(3) Structure beats scale. 'Hey Chat' (2026) shows frontier and Socratic-tuned LLMs fail at extended tutoring alone. A small policy over a prerequisite graph (which node next, how many turns) plus an LLM for the Socratic exchange wins on mastery rate and turns. Hooshyar et al. (2025) show LLM-only mastery estimates are temporally incoherent (wrong-direction updates) and argue for hybrid designs with an explicit learner model.

(4) Simulated students are useful but fragile. Prompted simulators perform poorly on realism (Scarlatos et al., ACL'26). They suffer from the 'competence paradox' (Yuan et al., 2026) and are sycophantic, with near-zero Selective Flip Score: they abandon a misconception after any correction, relevant or not (Do, Sonkar, Sachan, 2026). Fixes include an explicit epistemic-state spec, belief pinning, SFT/RL, history-conditioned profiles (Duan et al., EMNLP'26), knowledge-graph-sampled correctness (SSKG, 2026) and per-student trained simulators (StudentSim, 2026). Simulators still work well for reviewing tutor adaptivity across profiles (TeachTune, CHI'25), for stress-testing disengagement states such as gaming, wheel-spinning and off-task (DAS2, 2026), and as reward or ranking signals (Scarlatos et al., AIED'25).

Open debates: can LLM-only learner models be trusted, or must they be hybrid? How should simulator fidelity be validated (output similarity vs belief-faithfulness)? Automated tutor evaluation does not fully match human judgement. Most evidence comes from math and coding, so transfer to conceptual business content like OKR is untested, and a limitation worth stating openly.

Design implications for the GigaChat OKR tutor:
- Keep a hidden multi-call pipeline: an Analyzer (KC + correctness + misconception + affect/engagement state, as JSON), a deterministic learner model in Python (per-KC mastery, evidence count, hint level), a Planner (node, move from the EMT ladder or a contradiction trajectory), a Generator (one question, empathetic, no leakage), and a Verifier/best-of-n judge.
- Use a prerequisite graph of OKR KCs with mastery thresholds and turn budgets.
- Finish with a transfer task (write your own OKR) scored by rubric.
- Show a 'simulated learner' autopilot with ESS-card personas (misconception-holders, disengaged) and a contrastive SFS-style check, and state the simulator's limits openly.

State of the art (2024–2026). The field has converged on a simple lesson: one LLM that is prompted to be Socratic is not a reliable tutor. The strongest recent systems move pedagogical control out of the generating model into explicit, inspectable structure.
(1) An outer loop in code sequences the lesson. Examples: a finite-state transducer (MWPTutor, 2402.09216), a transition graph (StratL, 2410.03781), a prerequisite knowledge graph with a PPO sequencing policy (Tio et al., 2606.11744), a knowledge-mastery graph with gating (SHAPE, 2604.22134), and platform-enforced sequencing (Kestin et al., Sci. Rep. 2025, who state explicitly that a system prompt could not reliably scaffold multi-part problems).
(2) A grounding layer supplies the tutor with instructor-authored or auto-induced reference answers, rubrics and common misconceptions: Ruffle&Riley's tutoring script induced from a lesson text, Kestin's pre-written step-by-step solutions, the teacher solutions and mistakes in Bastani's GPT Tutor, and CS50's RAG over lecture captions.
(3) An analyzer runs before generation, verify-then-generate style (Daheim et al., 2407.09136), and tags knowledge components and correctness per turn (LLMKT, 2409.16490).
(4) A per-turn help contract comes from a non-LLM policy with a graded hint ladder (Pisan, 2608.12292). Help escalates on failure and fades on success (CoMeT, 2609.22993).
(5) A supervisor or critic layer covers leakage and off-topic drift. It combines deterministic filters, an LLM judge on risky turns, reasoning-before-response and multi-agent refinement (Zhao et al., ACL 2026, 2604.18660), and a two-stage injection guard (CS50). ExplainRoute (2609.03470) and Kadir's release-control work (2608.00515), both seen in search, push the same idea toward machine-checkable contracts for each response.

Deployment evidence supports guarded, structured tutors. Kestin et al.: 0.73–1.3 SD over active learning in less time. Bastani et al.: unguarded GPT-4 cut unassisted exam scores by 17%, while the guarded tutor removed the harm. Tutor CoPilot: +4 pp mastery, +9 pp for weaker tutors, fewer answer give-aways. LearnLM × Eedi: 76.4% of drafts approved with minimal edits and +5.5 pp on novel problems. World Bank Nigeria: +0.31 SD. The K-12 prompt-authoring deployment (2604.16738) shows that explicit finish lines and no-direct-answer rules measurably help, but LLM dialogues tend to drift toward lower cognitive demand.

Open debates.
(a) How much verification to use. More agents is not always better: a judge helped when upstream feedback was below 70% accurate but cost 4–6 pp when it was above 85% (2603.27076). Adaptive routing showed no reliable advantage over fixed Socratic strategies in ExplainRoute. Multi-agent latency compounds under load (ITAS latency study, 2604.24110), which matters for GigaChat's free tier.
(b) Orchestration versus training. Pedagogy can be baked into weights (LearnLM's pedagogical instruction following; RL-based tutors such as 2505.15607) or enforced by orchestration. For an API-only model like GigaChat, orchestration is the only available lever.
(c) Engagement versus learning. Ruffle&Riley found high engagement but no significant short-term gains over reading, so pipelines should be judged by post-dialogue transfer, not satisfaction.
(d) Robustness under sustained pressure. 'Scaffolding collapse' over long dialogues (2607.19371) and fine-tuned adversarial students show that leakage needs trajectory-level red-teaming. LLM-judged helpfulness does not substitute for pedagogy-targeted rubrics (2607.28128).

Implied design for the OKR demo on GigaChat:
- Offline: induce and freeze a concept map plus tutoring script from the OKR text, with questions, expected-answer rubric and misconception bank per node.
- Runtime, per turn: an analyzer call returns JSON (KC, correctness, misconception, affect/frustration, off-topic or answer-seeking flag). A deterministic controller then updates mastery, picks the node and sets the hint-ladder ceiling. A generator call is conditioned on the node's grounding, the diagnosis and the per-turn contract (one question, empathetic acknowledgement, no answer above the ceiling). A cheap regex check and a conditional LLM critic with at most one refine pass run only on risky turns.
- Finish line: the learner writes their own Objective and 2–3 measurable KRs, then a short unassisted check.
- Evaluation: scripted persona red-teaming (Pisan; Zhao et al.) and an MRBench-style pedagogical rubric.

Scope: 16 papers from arXiv, 2025-10 to 2026-09. Sweeps sorted by submittedDate: all:socratic (100 results, back to 2025-06), tutor+dialogue+LLM, 'intelligent tutoring'+LLM, pedagogical+LLM, tutoring+scaffolding/questioning, and empathy/sycophancy/self-explanation. Every abstract was read via id_list. Full text was checked for 2608.12292, 2603.23990 and 2606.11744 (help ladder, orchestrator rules, curriculum graph); 2602.02457's move table was spot-checked in its HTML.

STATE OF THE ART / CONSENSUS (late 2025 to 2026):

(1) Telling a single LLM to 'be Socratic' is not enough, and scale does not fix it.
- HeuristicEdu (2607.22996): an unaligned Qwen-72B scored 0% on Scaffolding Effectiveness with 96.7% keyword leakage.
- SafeTutors (2603.17373): pedagogical failures rise from 17.7% to 77.8% once the dialogue is multi-turn.
- Scaffolding collapse under pressure (2607.19371).
- Over-intervention: MetaCLASS (2602.02457) found silence was correct in 41.7% of turns but predicted only 4.2% of the time; Int-Bench (2607.21306) found LLMs intervene earlier and more often than humans and give complete solutions.
- Sycophancy and 'agreeable inaccuracies' (2605.14604, 2606.11744).

(2) The dominant architecture decouples pedagogical DECISION from WORDING. An explicit learner state (BKT, mastery bands, prerequisite graph) feeds a policy (rules, PPO, or a gating classifier) that picks a move or help ceiling. The LLM only writes the reply, and a checker or judge verifies it against a per-turn contract. Examples:
- ES-LLMs (2603.23990, AIED'26)
- Supervisor with an eight-rung help ladder (2608.12292)
- SLOW, which separates learner-state inference from action selection and adds prospective affect reasoning (2603.28062, AIED'26)
- Evidence-Decision-Feedback, with scaffold fading (2602.01415, AIED'26)
- SHAPE, which routes between instructing and problem-solving via a knowledge-mastery graph and resists 'pedagogical jailbreaks' (2604.22134, ACL'26)
- Curriculum graph plus PPO sequencer (2606.11744)

(3) Two alignment routes. The first is RL with multi-objective pedagogical rewards: PEARL (2605.29582), UCO (2511.08873), HeuristicEdu, and thinking rewards (2601.14560, where theory-grounded pedagogical reasoning prompting beats generic prompting). The second is training-free prompt optimization: 2605.27088 found all 12 prompt-optimised variants beat the strongest RL baseline. This makes a prompt-plus-orchestration pipeline on a closed API such as GigaChat a defensible, research-backed choice.

(4) Evidence that Socratic tutoring works, when it is well implemented:
- LearnLM RCT (2512.23633): +5.5 pp on novel-problem transfer.
- Socratic-Guidance vs Prompt-Refinement tutor (2607.03303, AIED'26 best paper): higher later learning gains and better independent LLM use.
- StudentBench (2609.28470): AI tutoring statistically equivalent to expert human tutoring on GRE learning gains.

OPEN DEBATES / COUNTER-EVIDENCE (worth presenting honestly to ML reviewers):
- Calibrating friction:
  - Socratic mode led to progressive disengagement and lower immediate gains in 2609.00584.
  - Socratic tutors with full context were rated least favourably in an RCT with n=132 (2609.29995).
  - A Socratic fact-checking chatbot's immediate gain (d=0.097) did not persist after a week (2609.32739).
  - Adaptive strategy routing showed no reliable advantage over fixed strategies in ExplainRoute (2609.03470).
  - Implication: use graduated help (a ladder with a mastery-based ceiling), switch to concrete elaboration when the learner is confused, and keep replies short, rather than questioning without end.
- Empathy: affective language showed no significant association with next-turn understanding (2607.08952). Polite and agentic language correlated negatively with rated quality (2512.20780). Warmth-heavy rewards produced agreeable inaccuracies. Yet mindful emotional support improved learning efficiency in Math with Matt (2609.02611). Consensus direction: 'kind but correct'. Empathy should target feelings and effort, never truth values, and should be brief.
- Evaluation validity: generic LLM-judge helpfulness is not a pedagogy signal (2607.28128). Prompted simulated students are unreliable (2601.04025, ACL'26), and LLMs simulating novices are over-coherent and overconfident (2602.01015). No frontier model exceeds 56% on TutorBench (2510.02663). Best practice is pedagogy-specific rubrics plus deterministic process metrics (leakage, learner-authored share, turns-to-mastery, collapse onset), several judges, scripted adversarial personas, and human spot checks.

DESIGN TAKEAWAYS FOR THE OKR/GigaChat PIPELINE:
- Keep an explicit concept graph of the OKR text with per-node mastery state.
- Plan the move before generating: a finite move set including metacognitive moves and 'minimal nudge'.
- Use a typed help ladder whose ceiling is set by code and never raised by the learner's text.
- Run a separate evaluator call that grades answers against the source text and resists social pressure.
- Run a post-generation contract check (no answer leakage, one question per turn, length budget).
- Open concepts with curiosity hooks (conflict or uncertainty); use revoicing plus pressing for reasoning.
- Switch to concrete examples when the learner is confused.
- Finish with a transfer task and a reflection move.
- Ship an evaluation harness with red-team personas: frustrated, answer-demanding, authority-claiming sycophancy probe, disengaged.

papers.title: Teaching a Large Language Model Tutor to Withhold the Answer: A Supervisor Architecture and an Evidence-Driven Method for Tuning Socratic Behavior
papers.authors: Yusuf Pisan
papers.summary: Reports a deployed programming tutor that makes answer-withholding a per-turn contract that a machine can check. A non-LLM policy core reads trusted learner state and sets a per-turn ceiling on an eight-rung help ladder. A deterministic detector strips solution code, and a separate LLM judge checks risky replies. Behaviour is tuned without human subjects: scripted student personas are driven through the live pipeline and re-scored by a stronger model, and the judge's stated rejection reason is recorded each time.
key_findings: A capable model pressed by a frustrated student does not withhold answers reliably from a prompt alone. The system therefore enforces withholding as a per-turn contract that a machine can check.

Architecture: a non-LLM policy core reads only trusted learner state and sets a per-turn ceiling on an eight-rung help ladder. A deterministic detector strips solution code, and a separate LLM judge checks each risky reply against the contract.

Tuning uses automated evaluation with no human subjects. Scripted student personas are driven through the live pipeline and re-scored by a stronger model, and the reason for each rejection is recorded so failures are fixed by cause.

This revealed an interpretable 'over-help ladder': blatant solution leaks, then naming the exact bug, then over-citing general facts, with each fix exposing the next. The tutor reached full compliance on all four acceptance criteria.

The paper cites a randomized study where an unguarded chatbot raised practice scores but lowered later unassisted test scores, while a Socratically guarded version kept the practice gain and removed the later loss.
practices: Compute the hint ceiling in Python from trusted learner state, not in the LLM. Adapt a multi-rung ladder to OKR (encourage, rephrase, point to the concept in the text, leading question, partial explanation, worked example about a different company, full model answer) and inject the current ceiling into GigaChat's hidden system prompt every turn.

Add a post-generation guard: a deterministic regex/keyword check against the hidden reference answer, plus a GigaChat judge call that rejects or rewrites any reply above the ceiling. Log the judge's reason so prompt fixes target causes.

Before the demo, run automated simulated-learner persona suites (for example earnest-but-stuck, 'just tell me the answer', social engineering, prompt injection) through the live pipeline and score them with a judge model.

papers.title: Hey Chat, Can You Teach Me? Structuring Socratic Dialogue for Human Learning in the Wild
papers.authors: Sidney Tio, Arunesh Sinha, Pradeep Varakantham
papers.summary: Argues that extended tutoring in open chat needs three skills at once: sequencing a curriculum, conducting Socratic dialogue, and inferring the student's knowledge state from the dialogue. Current LLMs fail to combine them. The authors separate the responsibilities. A prerequisite knowledge graph of subtopics is built per query, a lightweight PPO policy decides which node to teach next and how many turns to spend on it, and an LLM runs the Socratic exchange at that node and returns a student-progress signal.
key_findings: Frontier and education-tuned LLMs perform poorly at tutoring a student over an extended session, because the task requires sequencing a curriculum, conducting Socratic dialogue and inferring the student's knowledge state all at once. Scaling models alone does not close this gap.

The system separates these roles. It builds a prerequisite knowledge graph of subtopics, a lightweight PPO policy decides which node to teach next and for how many turns, and an LLM runs the Socratic exchange at that node and returns a signal of student progress.

Across held-out STEM and non-STEM topics, the PPO-paired tutor outperforms heuristic baselines, frontier general-purpose models and a Socratic-specialised model, both on the rate of full curriculum mastery and on the number of turns required.
Explicit curriculum structure delivers gains that scaling the underlying model does not.
practices: Break the OKR text into a small prerequisite graph (good Objective, then measurable Key Results, then outcome vs output/initiative, then ambition/scoring, then alignment). Let code pick the current node, and have GigaChat run only the Socratic exchange for that node.
Make GigaChat emit a hidden structured progress signal each turn, which the orchestrator uses to advance, stay or remediate.
Budget turns per node, and measure success as full mastery reached in few turns.

papers.title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
papers.authors: Xinmeng Hou, Yuxuan Weng, Chin Hsien Yeh, Ding Lin Lee, Lishan Zheng, Fang Li, Wuqi Wang, Yang Liu
papers.summary: Separates two things that 'giving less away' usually conflates: how much work the system carries (cognitive load) and what the learner must decide before help arrives (metacognitive demand). The principle is to hold the second constant and let the first vary. The CoMeT tutor raises support when a learner fails at a decision point and fades it once the learner takes the help up. In a within-subjects study, 131 adults used CoMeT, an unrestricted assistant and a question-only tutor on Python tasks.
key_findings: The paper separates cognitive load (how much work the system carries) from metacognitive demand (what the learner must decide before help arrives). Its principle holds demand constant and lets load vary: support rises when the learner fails at a decision point and fades on take-up.

In a within-subjects study, 131 adult learners worked on three Python tasks. CoMeT matched the question-only tutor's metacognitive demand, delivered artifacts twice as often as the unrestricted assistant, and frustrated learners less than the question-only tutor, with delegation and load unchanged.
Learners often did not answer the tutor. Fading held when the learner's turn addressed the decision under support.
CoMeT gave up the full answer in one session in sixteen, against one in six for the question-only tutor.
practices: Make help contingent: escalate the hint level only after a failed or empty attempt at the current decision point, and fade after successful take-up.
Keep the key decision with the learner even at high support. Vary the amount of content, not who owns the decision.
Avoid pure question-only tutoring. At higher rungs, give concrete artifacts such as a partial OKR template or a contrasting example to reduce frustration.
papers.verify_note: Verified via the arXiv API; metadata is correct. I added the full author list and the study size (131 learners).

papers.title: Guardrails or Roadblocks? Effects of Pedagogical Style and Context Awareness in AI Teaching Assistants for Programming
papers.authors: Madeleine Eastwood, Harshith Narne, Joseph Hilby, Paul Denny, Ashish Aggarwal, Amanpreet Kapoor
papers.summary: Randomized controlled trial with 132 introductory-programming students. Four AI teaching assistants crossed two dimensions: guidance style (Socratic vs direct instruction) and context awareness (none vs full problem plus student solution). The study measured perceptions, interaction behaviour and evidence of post-task comprehension.
key_findings: A randomized controlled trial with 132 introductory programming students used a 2x2 design: Socratic vs Direct guidance style, crossed with no context vs full context.
Students rated the Socratic assistant with full context least favorably, reporting significantly lower perceived support for task completion.

Descriptively, that condition had the highest interaction stress, the highest external LLM use and the lowest share of full-comprehension explanations. These differences were not statistically significant.
Guardrailed assistants are not automatically better for learning. Their effectiveness depends on balancing guidance and context in ways students find useful and worth continuing to use.
practices: Pair Socratic restraint with perceived helpfulness: acknowledge what is right, briefly explain why the tutor asks rather than tells, and offer a transparent escape hatch after N failed attempts.
Detect frustration signals ('just tell me', repeated 'I don't know') and move to a more supportive rung, so learners do not bypass the tutor for external LLMs.

papers.title: Mitigating Scaffolding Collapse in Socratic Tutors via Representation Alignment
papers.authors: Jing Shao, Qifeng Wu, Hanyu Zhang, Sixia Sun, Jun Zhuang
papers.summary: Defines 'scaffolding collapse': under sustained student pressure, a Socratic tutor gradually abandons guided inquiry and reveals solutions. The authors build Socratic dialogues across five STEM disciplines and synthesise collapsed negative trajectories for each. They then train with SFT warm-up, trajectory-weighted DPO and a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states.
key_findings: Scaffolding collapse: under sustained student pressure, a Socratic tutor gradually abandons guided inquiry and reveals solutions directly.
Prior defenses (prompting, preference optimization, filtering) only constrain observable responses. They leave unaddressed the internal representation drift that precedes trajectory-level collapse.
The method has two stages: SFT warm-up, then trajectory-weighted DPO plus a margin-preserving representation loss anchored to frozen reference states.

It was evaluated across five STEM disciplines and five red-teaming attack strategies. On Qwen3-8B it lowers Collapse Rate to 32%, delays average collapse onset beyond nine turns and keeps over-refusal low.
practices: Treat collapse as a trajectory-level risk. With an API-only model like GigaChat, where representation alignment is impossible, re-inject the Socratic contract and current state every turn rather than only at session start.
Red-team the tutor with persistent-pressure scripts of 10 or more turns, and check for over-refusal as well as answer leakage.

papers.title: SafeTutors: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy
papers.summary: A benchmark that evaluates safety and pedagogy of AI tutors together across mathematics, physics and chemistry. It uses a learning-science-grounded risk taxonomy of 11 harm dimensions and 48 sub-risks. The authors argue that the main tutoring risk is not toxic content but the quiet erosion of learning through answer over-disclosure, misconception reinforcement and abandoned scaffolding.
key_findings: The main tutoring risk is not toxic content. It is quiet erosion of learning through answer over-disclosure, misconception reinforcement and abandoned scaffolding.
The benchmark covers mathematics, physics and chemistry, with a taxonomy of 11 harm dimensions and 48 sub-risks.
All models show broad harm, and scale does not reliably help. Multi-turn dialogue worsens behavior: pedagogical failures rise from 17.7% to 77.8%.
Harms vary by subject, and single-turn 'safe/helpful' results can hide systematic tutor failure over extended interaction.
practices: Evaluate the tutor on full multi-turn simulated dialogues and report failure rates by turn index, not just single-reply quality.
Treat answer over-disclosure and misconception reinforcement as primary safety failures and guard against them explicitly in both the prompt and the critic.

papers.title: Reasoning Trajectories for Socratic Debugging of Student Code: From Misconceptions to Contradictions and Updated Beliefs
papers.authors: Erfan Al-Hossami, Razvan Bunescu
papers.summary: Formulates Socratic debugging as a guided Reasoning Trajectory (RT): a sequence that leads the student to a statement about program behaviour contradicting the misconception behind the bug. Reaching the contradiction should trigger cognitive dissonance and a lasting belief update. The paper introduces the reasoning-trajectory generation task and a dataset of debugging problems annotated with manual or LLM-generated trajectories, plus LLM methods for Socratic conversations anchored on those trajectories.
In a large-scale LLM-as-judge evaluation, large language and reasoning models generate up to 91% correct reasoning trajectories and 98.7% valid conversation turns.
practices: For each anticipated OKR misconception (for example 'KR = a list of tasks'), pre-author a hidden question chain that ends in a consequence contradicting that belief, then ask the learner to reformulate.
Plan the trajectory in a hidden step, then anchor each visible tutor question on the next step of that plan.

papers.title: Discerning minds or generic tutors? Evaluating instructional guidance capabilities in Socratic LLMs
papers.authors: Ying Liu, Can Li, Ting Zhang, Mei Wang et al.
papers.summary: Moves evaluation from Socratic question generation to adaptive instructional guidance. Existing LLMs often fail to provide effective adaptive scaffolding when learners experience confusion or require redirection.
A behavior-guided fine-tuning strategy using behavior-prompted instructional dialogues substantially enhances guidance performance.

Write dedicated handling for confusion and redirection, the states where the paper finds LLMs fail most (e.g. simplify, offer a contrasting example, return to a prerequisite).

papers.authors: Jiayu Liu, Zhenya Huang, Tong Xiao, Jing Sha, Jinze Wu, Qi Liu, Shijin Wang, Enhong Chen

Add a 'Dean'-style critic pass, a second model call with a checklist, that reviews and revises the tutor draft before the learner sees it.

StratL optimises LLM prompts to steer the model to follow a predefined multi-turn tutoring plan represented as a transition graph.

TreeInstruct uses a state space-based planning algorithm that estimates a student's conceptual and syntactical knowledge and dynamically builds a question tree, addressing independent and dependent mistakes concurrently.

papers.title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
papers.authors: Hamsa Bastani, Osbert Bastani, Alp Sungu et al.
papers.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) 122(26)
papers.summary: Field experiment giving nearly a thousand high-school math students GPT-4 tutors in two designs: a standard ChatGPT-like interface ('GPT Base') and a version with prompts designed to safeguard learning ('GPT Tutor'). Learning was measured after access was removed.

With access during practice, grades improved 48% for GPT Base and 127% for GPT Tutor.
When access was removed, students who had GPT Base performed worse than those who never had access (17% reduction); GPT Tutor's safeguards largely mitigated this negative effect.

papers.title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
papers.authors: Greg Kestin, Kelly Miller, Anna Klales, Timothy Milbourne, Gregorio Ponti
papers.summary: Randomized controlled trial in a college physics course. It compared a custom GPT-4 tutor, designed around the same pedagogical best practices as the in-class lessons, with in-class active learning. The paper also documents which best practices could be carried by the system prompt and which needed platform structure.

Put a hidden expert reference answer and rubric for each exercise into the system prompt. This grounds feedback and reduces hallucinated OKR advice.
