Question types follow Paul & Elder: Clarification, Probing assumptions, Probing reasons and evidences, Probing implications and consequences, Probing alternative viewpoints and perspectives, plus an added catch-all 'Others' for non-Socratic questions.
Automatic and human evaluation show the SoQG models can produce realistic, type-sensitive, human-like Socratic questions.
practices: For a conceptual, non-math topic like OKR, use the Paul-Elder types as the question bank: clarification, assumptions, evidence, implications and alternative viewpoints.
Have the orchestrator pick an explicit question type per turn and condition GigaChat on it. This diversifies questioning (the models were type-sensitive).
papers.verify_note: Verified on ACL Anthology and in the PDF (Table 1). Added the 110K dataset size from the abstract.

papers.title: Bridging the Novice-Expert Gap via Models of Decision-Making: A Case Study on Remediating Math Mistakes
papers.authors: Rose E. Wang, Qingyang Zhang, Carly Robinson, Susanna Loeb, Dorottya Demszky
papers.summary: Uses cognitive task analysis to turn an expert tutor's hidden reasoning into an explicit decision model for remediation. Before responding, the expert decides (A) the student's error type, (B) a remediation strategy and (C) the intention behind the response. The authors build a dataset of 700 real tutoring conversations annotated with these decisions and test whether conditioning LLMs on them improves responses.
key_findings: Bridge uses cognitive task analysis to turn an expert's latent thought process into a decision model: (A) the student's error, (B) a remediation strategy, (C) an intention, all decided before the response is generated.
Dataset: 700 real tutoring conversations annotated with expert decisions.

GPT-4 responses conditioned on expert decisions (e.g., 'simplify the problem') were preferred 76% more often than responses without them. Random decisions lowered GPT-4's response quality by 97% compared with expert decisions, so decisions must be context-sensitive.
practices: Have the model make a hidden decision step before each tutor reply, output as structured JSON: {learner_error, strategy, intention}. Condition generation on it and never show it to the learner.
Build a closed menu of remediation strategies mapped to common OKR misconceptions.
Log the decision triple per turn to support ablations (with vs. without decisions, or random decisions), mirroring the paper.
papers.verify_note: arXiv record matches (first posted Oct 2023; the paper appeared at NAACL 2024). Replaced the vague 'closes much of the gap' claim with the paper's actual method description.

papers.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
papers.authors: Rose E. Wang, Ana T. Ribeiro, Carly D. Robinson, Susanna Loeb, Dora Demszky
papers.summary: Deploys an LM system that uses a model of expert thinking (building on Bridge) to give live tutors expert-like suggestions. It was tested in a pre-registered randomised controlled trial with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students from under-served communities. Strategy use was analysed with classifiers over more than 550,000 messages.
key_findings: Pre-registered RCT with 900 tutors and 1,800 K-12 students. Students whose tutors had Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to master topics (p<0.01), and students of lower-rated tutors gained 9 p.p.
A classifier analysis of 550,000+ messages found that tutors with access used more high-quality strategies (e.g., asking guiding questions) and were less likely to give away the answer.
The cost was about $20 per tutor per year. Tutors flagged that some suggestions were not grade-level appropriate.
practices: Base the strategy layer on an explicit model of expert decision-making, the same mechanism the RCT validated.
Monitor 'guiding question' vs. 'giving the answer' rates automatically with a classifier or LLM judge over every GigaChat reply.
Include the learner's level in the state so vocabulary and examples fit the level.
papers.verify_note: Verified on arXiv. All numbers match the abstract. Added the sample sizes.

papers.title: LearnLM: Improving Gemini for Learning
papers.authors: LearnLM Team, Abhinit Modi, Aditya Srikanth Veerubhotla, Aliya Rysbek, et al.
papers.summary: Recasts pedagogical behaviour as 'pedagogical instruction following'. Training and evaluation examples carry system-level instructions that describe the pedagogy wanted in later turns, so teachers or developers specify pedagogy rather than having one definition baked into the model. Pedagogical data is added to Gemini's post-training mixture.
key_findings: Reframes pedagogy as pedagogical instruction following: system-level instructions describe the pedagogy attributes wanted. This avoids committing the model to a single definition of pedagogy and lets teachers or developers specify behaviour.

In expert evaluation across diverse learning scenarios, LearnLM was preferred with average preference strengths of +31% over GPT-4o, +11% over Claude 3.5 Sonnet and +13% over its base, Gemini 1.5 Pro.
practices: Since GigaChat cannot be post-trained here, use the same interface at inference: a hidden, detailed system prompt listing pedagogy attributes, plus per-turn instructions from the policy layer.
Keep the pedagogy specification declarative and editable (e.g., a YAML teaching card) so a teacher can change behaviour without touching code.
papers.verify_note: Verified on arXiv. Numbers match the abstract.

papers.title: Training LLM-based Tutors to Improve Student Learning Outcomes in Dialogues
papers.authors: Alexander Scarlatos, Naiming Liu, Jaewook Lee, Richard Baraniuk, Andrew Lan
papers.summary: Trains a tutor to produce utterances that maximise the chance of a correct next student response while following pedagogical principles. Candidate tutor utterances are scored by (1) an LLM-based student model predicting student correctness and (2) a GPT-4o pedagogical rubric. The resulting preferences train Llama 3.1 8B with DPO.
key_findings: Candidate tutor utterances are scored by (1) an LLM-based student model that predicts the chance of a correct student response and (2) a pedagogical rubric evaluated by GPT-4o. The resulting preferences train Llama 3.1 8B with DPO.

The trained model's utterances led to significantly higher predicted chances of correct student responses, while keeping pedagogical quality comparable to GPT-4o. Qualitative analysis and a human evaluation support this.
practices: Apply the recipe at inference without training: generate N candidate GigaChat replies, score each with a rubric judge and an outcome proxy, then send the best.
Use the same two-part score (outcome plus pedagogy) as the offline evaluation metric.
papers.verify_note: arXiv metadata verified. The AIED 2025 venue was not independently confirmed here (LNCS volume number unchecked), so I removed the volume number. I dropped the interpretive claim about avoiding single-signal optimisation and replaced it with the method as described in the abstract.

papers.title: LLMs Are Already Good Tutors: Training-Free Prompt Optimization for Pedagogical Math Tutoring
papers.authors: Unggi Lee, Minchul Shin, Yeil Jeong, Sookbun Lee, et al.
papers.summary: Asks whether evolving only the system prompt via API calls, with no weight updates, can replace RL-based pedagogical alignment. The authors adapt 7 published prompt-optimisation methods, propose 5 education-specialised ones (including ParetoGrad), and evaluate all 12 under 5 conditions on 2 out-of-distribution benchmark suites, with frozen tutor and student models.
key_findings: The study adapts 7 published and 5 new education-specialised prompt-optimisation methods, evaluated under 5 conditions on 2 OOD benchmark suites. All 12 best-per-method configurations beat the strongest RL-trained baseline (R_total = 0.633).
ParetoGrad gave the best Pareto balance across post-test solve rate, leak control and helpfulness, without dominating any single component.

An 82-code educational codebook showed that training-free methods use teaching-knowledge patterns at 2-3x the rate of RL-trained models, with a compensating ~10 percentage-point reduction in intent-level scaffolding.
practices: This supports the chosen setup: an API-only model can be pedagogically aligned through system-prompt optimisation alone, without fine-tuning.
Optimise the hidden prompt against a multi-objective score (progress, leakage, helpfulness) on simulated learners, and report the Pareto trade-off.
Counter the documented side effect, reduced intent-level scaffolding, by having the policy layer push questioning moves explicitly.
papers.verify_note: Verified on arXiv (submitted May 2026). Numbers match the abstract.

papers.title: PIVOT: Preference-based Intervention Vectors for Pedagogical Tutor Steering
papers.authors: Fares Fawzi, Jiaxu Zhao, Tanya Nazaretsky, Tanja Käser
papers.summary: Argues that tutors must choose when to scaffold, hint, give feedback, explain or invite reflection, and that prompting and training lack reliable inference-time control over these moves. PIVOT learns activation-steering vectors for a frozen LLM from a seven-category tutor-move taxonomy. The taxonomy covers behaviours such as feedback, pumping, focusing, hinting, prompting, assertion and metacognitive reflection, and the vectors are learned in a generate-label-optimise loop with a human-validated LLM judge.
key_findings: PIVOT is an activation-steering framework. It learns preference-based intervention vectors online for frozen LLM tutors, using a seven-category tutor-move taxonomy and a generate-label-optimise loop. A human-validated LLM judge identifies target and confusable non-target moves to build preference pairs.
On held-out and out-of-domain tutoring data, PIVOT controls tutor moves while preserving relevance and fluency. Its directions can be scaled, transferred and composed at inference time.
In a user study with 30 teachers, 73.3% preferred steered conversations over neutral baseline interactions using the same prompt, and rated the controls as clear, usable and pedagogically meaningful.
practices: Activation steering is not possible through the GigaChat API. Adopt a tutor-move taxonomy (scaffold, hint, feedback, explain, invite reflection, etc.) as the action space of the policy layer, and enforce it with per-turn instructions plus an LLM judge that checks the reply realised the target move.
Use 'confusable non-target moves' in the judge rubric (e.g., a hint that is really an explanation of the answer) to catch leakage disguised as help.
papers.verify_note: Verified via the arXiv API. Added the fourth author (Tanja Käser). The move list in the original practices (pump/focus/prompt/assertion...) is not stated in the abstract, so it was generalised. The claim that move-level control is teacher-legible was dropped because it is an interpretation, not a reported finding.

papers.title: AutoTutor and Family: A Review of 17 Years of Natural Language Tutoring
papers.authors: Benjamin D. Nye, Arthur C. Graesser, Xiangen Hu
papers.venue: International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 24(4): 427-469
papers.summary: Reviews AutoTutor, a natural-language tutor built around expectation- and misconception-tailored (EMT) dialogue. For a deep question, the tutor holds a list of expected good answers and known misconceptions, and uses semantic matching to track which expectations the student has covered. It covers each expectation through a graduated cycle of moves.
key_findings: For each expectation, AutoTutor gave a pump ('what else?'), then a hint, then a prompt, then an assertion (bottom-out). The cycle stopped as soon as the expectation was covered.

Good students needed only pumps or hints, while lower-ability students needed prompts or assertions. AutoTutor 2.0 made students restate their understanding even of a bottom-out assertion before continuing.
AutoTutor produced average learning gains of about 0.8 sigma over controls who read static materials for the same time.

AutoTutor 1.1 and 2.0 both showed about 0.5 sigma. Gains were 0.15 sigma on shallow questions, 0.28 sigma on deep questions and 0.64 sigma on cloze questions, which foreshadowed larger gains for deep reasoning. The review also highlights the value of adapting to the affect of low-knowledge learners.
practices: Represent the OKR material as a list of expectations (key ideas the learner must articulate) and misconceptions. Track coverage per expectation with an LLM judge instead of AutoTutor's semantic matching.
Use pump -> hint -> prompt -> assertion as the default escalation per expectation, and after any bottom-out explanation require the learner to restate it in their own words.
Focus the dialogue on deep 'why/how' questions, e.g. why KRs must be measurable outcomes rather than tasks.
papers.verify_note: Verified against the full text on ERIC (ED586834). Added the cloze figure (0.64 sigma) and the issue number. All numbers are confirmed.

papers.title: SLOW: Strategic Logical-inference Open Workspace for Cognitive Adaptation in AI Tutoring
papers.authors: Yuang Wei, Ruijia Li, Bo Jiang
papers.venue: AIED 2026 (27th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Education)
papers.summary: Argues that single-pass generative tutors conflate cognitive diagnosis, affect perception and pedagogical decision-making. SLOW is a dual-process framework that separates learner-state inference from instructional action selection in a transparent decision workspace. It combines causal evidence parsing from learner language, fuzzy cognitive diagnosis with counterfactual stability analysis, and prospective affective reasoning about how a move might change the learner's emotions.
key_findings: SLOW explicitly separates learner-state inference from instructional action selection. It combines causal evidence parsing, fuzzy cognitive diagnosis with counterfactual stability analysis, and prospective affective reasoning about how choices may affect learners' emotional trajectories.
Hybrid human-AI judgments showed significant improvements in personalisation, emotional sensitivity and clarity.
Ablation studies confirmed that each module is needed, and a visualised decision-making process makes tutoring decisions interpretable.
practices: Add an affect channel to the state tracker (e.g., frustrated / confused / bored / confident), and let it change the move: acknowledge feelings, lower the rung, or switch to a concrete example.
Before choosing a move, anticipate how the learner is likely to feel after it (prospective affective reasoning), for example to avoid over-questioning a frustrated learner.
Show the decision workspace (diagnosis -> affect -> chosen move -> rationale) in a collapsible panel in the Streamlit UI.
papers.verify_note: Verified via the arXiv API. The arXiv comment confirms the venue as the 27th AIED conference. The metadata was correct.

papers.title: Large Language Models Approach Expert Pedagogical Quality in Math Tutoring but Differ in Instructional and Linguistic Profiles
papers.authors: Ramatu Oiza Abdulsalam, Segun Aroyehun
papers.summary: Compares expert tutors, novice tutors and seven LLMs responding to the same student math errors. It analyses instructional strategies (uptake such as restating and revoicing, pressing for accuracy and reasoning) and linguistic features (length, lexical diversity, readability, politeness, agency), and relates them to rated pedagogical quality.
key_findings: Larger LLMs generally receive higher pedagogical quality ratings and approach expert tutors on average. However, they underuse the discursive strategies of expert tutors and produce longer, more lexically diverse and more polite responses.
Pressing for accuracy and reasoning, restating/revoicing and lexical diversity were positively associated with perceived pedagogical quality.
Higher levels of agentic and polite language were negatively associated with perceived quality.
practices: Tell the generator to revoice the learner's idea and then press for reasoning or evidence ('How would you measure that?').
Limit reply length and excessive politeness or praise, and avoid agentic language where the tutor does the work.
Add these features (revoicing, press-for-reasoning, length, politeness) to the automatic per-turn rubric.
papers.verify_note: Verified via the arXiv API (v3). All claims are supported by the abstract.

papers.title: Unifying AI Tutor Evaluation: An Evaluation Taxonomy for Pedagogical Ability Assessment of LLM-Powered AI Tutors
papers.authors: Kaushal Kumar Maurya, KV Aditya Srivatsa, Kseniia Petukhova, Ekaterina Kochmar
papers.summary: The authors propose an 8-dimension taxonomy grounded in learning science for judging single tutor responses to a student mistake or confusion: mistake identification, mistake location, revealing of the answer, providing guidance, actionability, coherence, tutor tone and human-likeness. They release MRBench (192 math dialogues, 1,596 responses from 7 LLM tutors plus novice and expert humans) with gold human labels, and test whether Prometheus2 and Llama-3.1-8B can act as judges.
key_findings: The paper proposes an 8-dimension taxonomy and releases MRBench: 192 conversations and 1,596 responses from seven LLM-based and human tutors, with gold annotations.
Human annotators reached an average Cohen's kappa of 0.71 (substantial agreement). A pilot study gave a Fleiss' kappa of 0.65.
GPT-4 reveals the answer about 47% of the time, which makes its responses less suitable for tutoring.
Correlations between the LLM judges (Prometheus2, Llama-3.1-8B) and human annotations were mostly negative, except for human-likeness.
Tutor responses tend to be more neutral than encouraging, and no offensive responses were found from any LLM or human tutor.
practices: Use the 8 dimensions as a per-turn checklist in the hidden system prompt: identify the mistake, locate it, do not reveal the answer, give guidance, be actionable, stay coherent, keep an encouraging tone, sound human-like.
Write a post-hoc evaluator that labels each tutor turn on these dimensions (Yes / To some extent / No).
Do not trust a generic LLM judge. Calibrate it on a small human-labelled set and report the agreement.
papers.verify_note: Verified via the arXiv API (journal_ref NAACL 2025) and the full-text PDF: kappa 0.71, GPT-4 about 47%, negative judge correlations except human-likeness, neutral tone and no offensive responses are all confirmed. The claim 'even human tutors fall short' was removed as unverified.

papers.title: Findings of the BEA 2025 Shared Task on Pedagogical Ability Assessment of AI-powered Tutors
papers.authors: Ekaterina Kochmar, Kaushal Kumar Maurya, Kseniia Petukhova, KV Aditya Srivatsa, Anaïs Tack
papers.venue: 20th Workshop on Innovative Use of NLP for Building Educational Applications (BEA 2025, ACL)
papers.summary: This shared task turned four dimensions of the Maurya taxonomy into automatic classification tracks: mistake identification, mistake location, providing guidance and actionability. A fifth track asked systems to identify which tutor wrote a response. It summarises more than 50 international teams scored against gold human annotations.
key_findings: More than 50 teams took part across five tracks: mistake identification, mistake location, providing guidance, actionability and tutor identity.
Best macro-F1 on the four 3-class pedagogical tracks ranged from 58.34 (providing guidance) to 71.81 (mistake identification), which leaves significant room for improvement.
The best F1 on the 9-class tutor-identification track was 96.98.
practices: Treat automatic pedagogical judgments, especially of guidance quality, as noisy (best macro-F1 about 0.58). Combine an LLM judge with deterministic checks and human spot checks.
Put most design effort into correct, relevant guidance and a clear next step for the learner.
papers.verify_note: Verified via the arXiv API. Added the fifth author (Anaïs Tack). The claim that actionability is among the hardest dimensions is not stated in the abstract (only guidance is the lowest), so it was dropped.

papers.title: MathTutorBench: A Benchmark for Measuring Open-ended Pedagogical Capabilities of LLM Tutors
papers.authors: Jakub Macina, Nico Daheim, Ido Hakimi, Manu Kapur, Iryna Gurevych, Mrinmaya Sachan
papers.summary: An open benchmark that groups tutor abilities into three areas: expertise (problem solving, Socratic questioning), student understanding (judging solution correctness, locating and correcting mistakes) and pedagogy (scaffolding generation, pedagogical instruction following, each with a harder long-dialogue variant). A trained pedagogical reward model scores open-ended tutor turns by win rate against human teacher responses.
key_findings: A trained pedagogical reward model separates expert from novice teacher responses with high accuracy.
Subject expertise (solving ability) does not directly translate into good teaching. Pedagogy and expertise form a trade-off that depends on how specialised the model is for tutoring.
Tutoring becomes harder in longer dialogues, where simpler questioning strategies begin to fail. In the paper, only LearnLM keeps consistent performance.

It includes a pedagogical instruction-following task based on the LearnLM 'extended' prompt, which lists behaviours such as nudging students and asking guiding questions. Most models showed limited ability to follow pedagogical instructions.
practices: Evaluate the tutor on long, multi-turn dialogues, not just the first reply, and re-inject pedagogical rules and dialogue state every turn.
Keep solving and teaching as separate roles: a hidden expert step holds the model answer and rubric, and the visible tutor turn only scaffolds.
Build a small OKR-specific benchmark (spot a bad KR, locate the flaw, produce a scaffolding question) with each part scored separately.
papers.verify_note: Verified via arXiv, the full text and the ACL Anthology (EMNLP 2025 main, pp. 204-221). Added the missing authors (Kapur, Gurevych, Sachan). 'Oral' could not be confirmed and was dropped. 'General models degrade faster than specialised ones' was replaced with the paper's actual statement that only LearnLM stays consistent.

papers.title: Evaluating Gemini in an arena for learning
papers.authors: LearnLM Team, Abhinit Modi, Aditya Srikanth Veerubhotla, Aliya Rysbek, Andrea Huber, Ankit Anand et al.
papers.summary: In a blind, head-to-head, multi-turn 'arena for learning', 189 educators role-played realistic learning scenarios with two models and 206 pedagogy experts judged which model better supported the learner. Separate rubric-based ratings covered five pedagogy principles, each broken into concrete items.
key_findings: In an 'arena for learning', 189 educators role-played realistic learning use cases in blind, head-to-head, multi-turn comparisons of two models, and 206 pedagogy experts judged which model better supported the learner's goals.
Models compared were Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, GPT-4o and OpenAI o3. Excluding ties, experts preferred Gemini 2.5 Pro in 73.2% of match-ups, ranking it first overall.
Gemini 2.5 Pro also scored markedly higher across key principles of good pedagogy.
practices: Evaluate the tutor with blind, pairwise, multi-turn comparisons judged against pedagogy principles, not single-turn answer quality.
Use a principle-based pedagogy rubric (e.g. cognitive load, active learning, metacognition, curiosity, adaptivity) as both design spec and evaluation lens.
papers.verify_note: Metadata confirmed via arXiv API. Removed claims about the exact five-principle list, specific rubric items and the two-stage protocol, since they are not in the abstract that was read; kept only abstract-supported numbers (N=189/206, 73.2%). Practices generalised accordingly.

papers.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
papers.authors: LearnLM Team, Eedi, Albert Wang, Aliya Rysbek, Andrea Huber et al.
papers.summary: An exploratory randomised controlled trial with 165 students in five UK secondary schools. LearnLM, a model fine-tuned for pedagogy, drafted chat-tutoring messages on the Eedi maths platform, and expert tutors supervised and could edit every message before it was sent. Learning outcomes were compared with human-only tutoring.
key_findings: Exploratory RCT with N=165 students in five UK secondary schools; LearnLM drafted tutoring messages on the Eedi maths platform under expert tutor supervision.
Supervising tutors approved 76.4% of LearnLM's drafted messages with zero or minimal edits (one or two characters).

Students supported by LearnLM performed at least as well as those with human tutors on every measured outcome, and were 5.5 percentage points more likely to solve novel problems on subsequent topics (66.2% vs 60.7%).
In interviews, tutors highlighted LearnLM's Socratic questions as encouraging deeper reflection; multiple tutors reported learning new pedagogical practices from it.
practices: Cite as real-world evidence that pedagogically steered, Socratic LLM tutoring (with human supervision) can match human tutors.
Measure transfer: end the session with a new case the learner must solve alone, not just recall.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via arXiv API; all claims match abstract. Added N=165 and the human-supervision context (drafts were reviewed by tutors), which qualifies the result.

papers.title: Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models
papers.authors: Shuyi Fan, Boyuan Deng, Mengyu Xu, Jiale Liu, Hongyang Zhang, Qiaoxin Yang et al.
papers.summary: A pre-registered study of whether a general 'helpfulness' rubric scored by an LLM judge can tell direct answer-giving apart from pedagogical guidance. On three tutor bases, conversational and pedagogical policies built on the same model were paired with a fixed weak simulated student. The 1,179 answer-phase turns were scored by a frozen, condition-blind primary judge, then audited by a second judge. Deterministic detectors measured answer leakage and the student's independent work on the next turn.
key_findings: Pre-registered audit comparing conversational vs pedagogical policies on the same base model across three tutor bases, with a fixed weak simulated student and 1,179 confirmatory answer-phase tutor turns.
On the primary base (primary judge Claude Opus 4.8), the policies did not differ significantly in helpfulness but were perfectly rank-separated by the pedagogy rubric (Cliff's |delta| 0.10 vs 1.0).
Across two judges (robustness judge GPT-5.6 Sol), pedagogy contrasts kept their direction where detected, while the helpfulness ordering reversed between judges on two of three bases.
On every base, answer-revealing turns were followed by less independent student work (judge-invariant deterministic measure).
Conclusion: general-purpose helpfulness is not a reliable pedagogy signal; tutor evaluation should pair pedagogy-targeted rubrics with deterministic process measures.
practices: Do not evaluate or optimise the tutor with a generic helpfulness judge; use a pedagogy-specific rubric.
Add deterministic process metrics next to any LLM judge, such as an answer-leakage detector and next-turn independent work by the learner.
Use a frozen, condition-blind judge prompt and a second judge model as a robustness check.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via arXiv API (v2, July 2026). Claims match abstract. Removed 'learner's share of words' from practices since the paper's named deterministic measures are answer leakage and next-turn independent work.

papers.title: TutorBench: A Benchmark To Assess Tutoring Capabilities Of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Rakshith S Srinivasa, Zora Che, Chen Bo Calvin Zhang, Diego Mares, Ernesto Hernandez, Jayeon Park et al.
papers.summary: 1,490 expert-curated high-school and AP tutoring samples across three tasks: adaptive explanations tailored to a student's confusion, actionable feedback on student work, and active learning through hint generation. Each sample has its own rubric, which an LLM judge applies.
key_findings: TutorBench has 1,490 expert-curated high-school/AP samples across three tasks: adaptive explanations for student confusion, actionable feedback on student work, and hint generation for active learning, each with sample-specific rubrics judged by an LLM judge.
Of 16 frontier LLMs evaluated, none scored above 56%.
All frontier models achieved under a 60% pass rate on rubric criteria related to guiding, diagnosing and supporting students.
Claude models outperformed others on supporting active learning but lagged on the other two use cases.
practices: Write sample-specific rubrics for each exercise and use them with an LLM judge rather than generic criteria.
Cover all three tutoring moves: adaptive explanation after confusion, actionable feedback on the learner's draft, and graded hints.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via arXiv API; claims match abstract. Softened the claim that sample-specific rubrics make judging 'much more reliable' (abstract only calls the method reliable and fine-grained).

papers.title: Evaluating Answer Leakage Robustness of LLM Tutors against Adversarial Student Attacks
papers.authors: Jin Zhao, Marta Knežević, Tanja Käser
papers.summary: The authors study learners who try to extract the final answer. They adapt six groups of adversarial and persuasive techniques to tutoring and test a broad set of LLM tutors, including pedagogically aligned models and a multi-agent design, for answer leakage.
key_findings: Evaluates LLM tutors (several families, pedagogically aligned models, and a multi-agent design) under six groups of adversarial and persuasive techniques adapted to education, measuring whether the tutor reveals the final answer.
In-context adversarial student agents often fail to carry out effective attacks.
The authors fine-tune an adversarial student agent to jailbreak tutors and propose it as the core of a standardised tutor-robustness benchmark.
Simple but effective defence strategies reduce answer leakage and strengthen tutor robustness.
practices: Include adversarial/persuasive student personas in the evaluation suite and measure the answer-leakage rate.
Note that prompted red-team students likely underestimate leakage risk.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via arXiv API; comment field says ACL 2026. Dropped the 'empathy plus smaller step' practice since the abstract does not specify the defence strategies.

papers.title: Simulated Students in Tutoring Dialogues: Substance or Illusion?
papers.authors: Alexander Scarlatos, Jaewook Lee, Simon Woodhead, Andrew Lan
papers.summary: The paper formally defines the student-simulation task, proposes metrics covering linguistic, behavioural and cognitive fidelity, and benchmarks many simulation methods on a real maths tutoring dialogue dataset, with both automated and human evaluation.
key_findings: Many LLM-tutoring works use simulated students (often via simple prompting) for training and evaluation, but little work measures their quality.
The paper formally defines student simulation and proposes linguistic, behavioural and cognitive evaluation metrics, benchmarked on a real-world math tutoring dialogue dataset.
Automated and human evaluation show prompting strategies perform poorly; supervised fine-tuning and preference optimisation do much better but remain limited.
practices: State openly that prompted simulated learners are a weak proxy; use them for regression and robustness testing, not as proof of learning gains.
Add some real human test dialogues alongside simulated ones.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via arXiv API (comment: Published in ACL 2026). Full author list is four authors; kind corrected to peer-reviewed venue.

papers.title: Simulating Students or Sycophantic Problem Solving? On Misconception Faithfulness of LLM Simulators
papers.authors: Heejin Do, Shashank Sonkar, Mrinmaya Sachan
papers.summary: The authors propose a controlled framework for testing whether an LLM student simulator keeps a misconception-driven belief state and updates it only when feedback targets that misconception. Targeted feedback is compared with misaligned and generic controls using a new Selective Flip Score (SFS). They then post-train simulators with SFT, preference optimisation and RL.
key_findings: Introduces a misconception-contrastive feedback protocol (targeted vs misaligned vs generic feedback) and the Selective Flip Score (SFS).
Across seven LLMs (4B-120B), multiple datasets and prompting strategies, simulators show near-zero SFS, correcting answers at similarly high rates regardless of feedback relevance.
The failure is sycophantic: models act like problem-solvers who treat any corrective signal as a cue to abandon the simulated belief.
Misconception faithfulness is trainable: SFT yields gains up to +0.56, and SFS-aligned RL gives more consistent improvements than preference optimisation.
practices: Give each simulated learner an explicit misconception and check that it is retained unless the tutor addresses it, since prompted simulators tend to drop it on any correction.
Include a control comparing targeted probes against generic 'that's wrong' feedback when evaluating with simulated learners.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via arXiv API; claims match abstract.

papers.title: Simulating Disengaged Students to Evaluate LLM-based Tutors
papers.authors: Xianghui Meng, Jionghao Lin
papers.summary: DAS2 is a reproducible pre-deployment protocol that simulates five learner-engagement states (engaged, gaming the system, wheel-spinning, off-task, mixed) and evaluates AI tutors in each. It is validated against human-labelled ASSISTments09 sessions.
key_findings: Proposes DAS2 (Disengagement-Aware Student Simulators), a pre-deployment protocol that models five learner-engagement states: engaged, gaming, wheel-spinning, off-task and mixed.
On 100 sampled ASSISTments09 sessions, two human coders agreed on 84% (Cohen's kappa 0.78). Among agreed cases, DAS2 rule-based labels matched human consensus in 81% (kappa 0.75).
Conditioning simulations on the intended learner state cut the correctness-rate gap between simulated and authentic sessions from 0.54 to 0.20 for gaming and from 0.51 to 0.18 for wheel-spinning.
A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B better matched authentic response-time distributions, while prompt-only GPT-4o produced more distinguishable learner states.
Five AI tutors (from the Claude, Llama, Gemini, Qwen and GPT families) kept stable relative rankings across learner states and interaction lengths, but absolute performance varied by state.
Human validation showed that automated tutor evaluation does not fully align with human judgment.
practices: Build the persona suite around engagement states as well as knowledge states: an engaged learner, one gaming for answers, one wheel-spinning, one off-task, and a mixed one.

Add per-state tutor policies to the hidden prompt, for example re-engaging an off-task learner, shrinking the step for a wheel-spinning one, and redirecting a gaming learner without giving away the answer.
Do not rely only on LLM-as-judge scores; spot-check them with human ratings.
papers.verify_note: Verified against the arXiv API: the id, title, both authors and the 2026 date match. Findings were checked against the abstract, and the claim that simulator choice (Qwen fine-tune vs GPT-4o prompting) matters was added. The specific per-state tactics in the practices (such as a worked analogy) are design suggestions, not results from the paper.

papers.title: Rethinking Scaffolding in LLM Tutors: The Interactional Mismatch Between Benchmarks and Real-World Deployments
papers.authors: Alexandra Neagu, Jeffrey T. H. Wong, Marcus Messer, Rhodri Nelson, Peter B. Johnson
papers.summary: The authors define two metrics, Chatbot Scaffolding and Student Uptake, and apply them to 9,490 chats from nine datasets covering AI-tutor benchmarks and real deployments of educational chatbots.
key_findings: Introduces two metrics, Chatbot Scaffolding and Student Uptake, and applies them to nine datasets totalling 9,490 chats, covering both AI-tutor benchmarks and real-world educational chatbot deployments.
Benchmarks assume a high-scaffolding, high-uptake environment, while real students show lower uptake overall.
Real students often bypass the chatbot's pedagogical framing to push the conversation towards their own learning goals, at little interpersonal cost.

The authors argue that bypassing scaffolding is not necessarily harmful. It often signals a mismatch between the chatbot's framing and the student's goals, and future benchmarks should evaluate how tutors handle student-driven interaction.
practices: Measure student uptake, not only whether the tutor scaffolds: does the learner actually engage with the Socratic question?
Negotiate the goal explicitly at session start and let the learner redirect. Treat bypass attempts as a signal to adapt rather than something to suppress rigidly.
papers.verify_note: Verified against the arXiv API: the id, title and 2026 date match, and the arXiv comment confirms the venue as Pluralistic Alignment Workshop @ ICML 2026 (Seoul). The full author list is now given (Nelson and Johnson added), and the dataset size (9 datasets, 9,490 chats) comes from the abstract.

papers.title: The Socratic Elenchus
papers.authors: Gregory Vlastos
papers.venue: Oxford Studies in Ancient Philosophy, vol. 1, pp. 27-58
papers.summary: The classic analytic account of Socratic refutation (elenchus), which launched the long-running debate over what the elenchus can actually establish. Bibliographic record confirmed on PhilPapers. The content below comes from the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Socrates' (J. M. Ambury), which summarises Vlastos and explains elenchus, maieutics and dialectic.
key_findings: Vlastos characterises the elenchus in Plato's early dialogues as a cross-examination of the interlocutor's own thesis. Socrates gets agreement to further premises, then shows that they are inconsistent with the thesis.

He poses the 'problem of the Socratic elenchus': the procedure only shows inconsistency between the thesis and other agreed premises, yet Socrates treats it as establishing that the thesis is false. Vlastos argues that Socrates relies on elenchus for positive ethical conclusions as well as refutations.
The same volume contains a reply by Richard Kraut (pp. 59-70) and Vlastos's own 'Afterthoughts on the Socratic Elenchus' (pp. 71-74).
practices: Model the dialogue as elicit, test, reconstruct. Ask the learner for their own definition (for instance 'what makes a good Key Result?'), test it against premises they already accepted, and then help them rebuild it.
Refute through the learner's own commitments rather than tutor authority, for instance 'you said a KR must be measurable, so is "improve customer happiness" a KR?'.
Unlike many of the dialogues, which end without a conclusion, add a consolidation step after each impasse.
papers.verify_note: Existence and venue were confirmed through PhilPapers and web search results; the PhilPapers page itself returned 403, and the metadata is correct. The claims about maieutics (Theaetetus 150b-151b) and about dialectic as the constructive complement were removed from key_findings because they come from encyclopedia summaries (IEP), not from this paper. The constructivist vs non-constructivist framing comes from the later secondary literature, so it was folded into the description of the problem. The consolidation practice is a design inference.

papers.title: The Thinker's Guide to the Art of Socratic Questioning
papers.authors: Richard Paul, Linda Elder
papers.venue: Foundation for Critical Thinking (Thinker's Guide Library), Dillon Beach, CA
papers.summary: A practitioner guide that systematises Socratic questioning into types of probing questions tied to the elements of reasoning. It is the taxonomy that most NLP work on Socratic questions cites. The category list below is taken from Ang et al. (EACL 2023, Table 1), which reproduces the Paul and Elder taxonomy.
key_findings: A short practitioner guide on the mechanics of Socratic dialogue, the critical-thinking concepts it relies on, and the role of questioning in developing a disciplined mind.
It presents Socratic questioning as a way to uncover the beliefs, assumptions and reasoning behind a statement, not as fact-quizzing.

It is commonly operationalised as a taxonomy of question types: clarification, probing assumptions, probing reasons and evidence, probing implications and consequences, and probing viewpoints and perspectives. Paul's original scheme also includes questions about the question.
practices: Use the taxonomy as a closed inventory of question moves and choose one type per tutor turn: clarification for vague answers, assumptions or evidence for unsupported claims, implications to test an OKR, viewpoints for other stakeholders.
Log the question type of every tutor turn so reviewers can audit coverage and diversity.
Map types onto OKR content, for instance 'if the team hits this KR, is the Objective achieved?'.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed through WorldCat and catalogue listings: Foundation for Critical Thinking, Dillon Beach CA, 2006, ISBN 0944583318. The PhilPapers URL returned 403, so the URL was switched to WorldCat. The exact five-category wording is a common secondary operationalisation that could not be checked against the book text, so it is hedged.

papers.title: The 2 Sigma Problem: The Search for Methods of Group Instruction as Effective as One-to-One Tutoring
papers.authors: Benjamin S. Bloom
papers.summary: Reports the Anania and Burke dissertation studies (grades 4, 5 and 8; probability and cartography; 11 periods over 3 weeks), in which students were randomly assigned to conventional classes, mastery learning, or one-to-one tutoring combined with formative tests and corrective feedback. Frames the challenge of finding scalable methods as effective as tutoring.
key_findings: Reporting studies by his students Anania and Burke, Bloom found that the average tutored student scored about 2 SD above the conventional-class average, outperforming about 98% of control students.
Mastery learning in groups (formative tests plus correctives) gave about 1 SD, above about 84% of control students.
About 90% of tutored students reached the level attained by only the top 20% of conventionally taught students.
The tutoring condition was combined with mastery-learning procedures (formative tests and feedback-correctives).
practices: Treat the tutor as tutoring plus mastery learning: each topic ends with a formative check, with a corrective loop until it is passed.
Present 2 sigma as motivation, not as a promise. VanLehn (2011) found human tutoring at about d = 0.79.
papers.verify_note: Metadata confirmed through Crossref (vol. 13, issue 6, pp. 4-16, June 1984). The abstract is not available through the API. The numbers were checked against multiple secondary summaries and the Wikipedia article on the 2 sigma problem; a PDF copy exists on gwern.net.

papers.title: The Relative Effectiveness of Human Tutoring, Intelligent Tutoring Systems, and Other Tutoring Systems
papers.authors: Kurt VanLehn
papers.summary: A review of experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring (classified by interaction granularity: answer-based, step-based, substep-based) and no tutoring. It tests the common belief that finer interaction granularity always means more learning.
key_findings: A review of experiments comparing human tutoring, computer tutoring (answer-based, step-based and substep-based) and no tutoring.
Contrary to the belief that answer-based systems, ITS and human tutors reach d = 0.3, 1.0 and 2.0, human tutoring came out at d = 0.79.
Intelligent tutoring systems reached d = 0.76, nearly as effective as human tutoring.

The widely held belief that effectiveness rises as interaction granularity gets finer was not confirmed. Beyond step-level interaction, the gains level off, which VanLehn calls the interaction plateau.
practices: Design at the step level: one tutor turn should target one idea, not word-by-word fill-in. Over-fragmenting the material into micro-questions is unlikely to add learning.
Report realistic targets: aim for ITS-level effects (about d = 0.76) rather than claiming 2 sigma.
papers.verify_note: Metadata confirmed through Crossref and the ERIC abstract (EJ946764). The Nye et al. (2014) citation was dropped because it is not part of this paper. The interaction-plateau wording is based on the paper body, which is consistent with the abstract's statement that the granularity belief was not confirmed.

papers.title: Learning from human tutoring
papers.authors: Michelene T. H. Chi, Stephanie A. Siler, Heisawn Jeong, Takashi Yamauchi, Robert G. Hausmann
papers.summary: Tests tutor-centred, student-centred and interactive hypotheses of why tutoring works. In a second study, tutors were forbidden from giving explanations and feedback and were instead encouraged only to prompt students, to force an interactive rather than didactic dialogue.
key_findings: Tests three hypotheses for why tutoring works (tutor-centred, student-centred and interactive). In a second study, tutors were suppressed from giving explanations and feedback and were encouraged to prompt instead.
Students learned just as effectively when tutors were suppressed from explaining and giving feedback.
Learning in the interactive style is attributed to deeper and more numerous scaffolding episodes, and to students taking more control of their own learning by reading more.
What students learned from reading was limited by their reading abilities.
practices: Default to prompting, not explaining: the main tutor moves are prompts, scaffolding questions and pointers back to the text, with explanations as a fallback.
Encourage the learner to go back to the source text themselves instead of quoting it for them.
Keep a bottom-out explanation path, because learning through prompting and reading is limited by the learner's reading ability.
papers.verify_note: Metadata confirmed through Crossref (all five authors, vol. 25, issue 4, pp. 471-533). The abstract was retrieved from OpenAlex and supports all the findings. 'Rereading' was changed to 'reading more' to match the abstract.

papers.title: The ICAP Framework: Linking Cognitive Engagement to Active Learning Outcomes
papers.authors: Michelene T. H. Chi, Ruth Wylie
papers.summary: Defines four modes of cognitive engagement from overt learner behaviour (Interactive, Constructive, Active, Passive) and hypothesises that learning increases from Passive to Interactive. Validated on note taking, concept mapping and self-explaining studies.
key_findings: ICAP classifies engagement by overt behaviour into Interactive, Constructive, Active and Passive modes, and hypothesises that learning increases I > C > A > P.
Constructive responses require generating output beyond the given material (e.g. explaining, generating examples). Merely agreeing or repeating counts as Active at most.

A dialogue counts as Interactive only when both partners' contributions are primarily constructive with sufficient turn taking. If one partner dominates and the other only agrees or backchannels, it is not interactive in the ICAP sense.
Frequent turn taking is argued to help integrate small pieces of new knowledge, a mechanism similar to that proposed for self-explanation.
practices: Avoid yes/no and 'do you agree?' questions. Every tutor question should require the learner to generate content: explain, give an example, write an OKR, critique one.
Keep tutor turns short so the learner produces most of the substantive content.
Build on the learner's contribution in each turn (paraphrase it, then extend) to approach the Interactive mode.
Use the ICAP mode of learner utterances as an evaluation metric, for example the share of learner turns that are constructive.
papers.verify_note: Existence and metadata confirmed (T&F DOI 10.1080/00461520.2014.965823, ASU LCL page). Findings slightly generalised: the specific claim about pumps/hints eliciting constructive responses was folded into a broader, safer statement since it could not be checked word for word.

papers.title: Confusion can be beneficial for learning
papers.authors: Sidney D'Mello, Blair Lehman, Reinhard Pekrun, Arthur Graesser
papers.summary: Two experiments in which learners held trialogues with animated tutor and peer agents about flawed scientific studies. Confusion was induced by having the agents contradict each other or present incorrect information, testing the claim that cognitive disequilibrium helps learning if it is induced, regulated and resolved.
key_findings: Confusion was induced with contradictions (e.g. agents disagreeing) during learning of difficult conceptual topics. When the contradictions actually confused learners, performance on multiple-choice post-tests and on transfer tests was substantially higher.
Confusion is beneficial when it is appropriately regulated and resolved, because it prompts deeper processing of the material. Otherwise it risks turning into frustration.
practices: Operationalise aporia as a controlled 'contradiction' move: present a plausible but flawed OKR, or two conflicting views, and ask the learner to judge. Use it sparingly.
Always pair a confusion-inducing move with a resolution path (hints, then a consolidation summary). Watch for frustration signals and switch to support.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via ScienceDirect and Google Scholar. Added missing fourth author Arthur Graesser. Dropped the unverifiable reference to Nye et al. 2014 and the 'flaws in case studies' detail; findings rephrased to match the ScienceDaily summary and abstract.

papers.title: When Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Works: Evidence for Productive Failure
papers.authors: Tanmay Sinha, Manu Kapur
papers.summary: A meta-analysis of 53 studies and 166 comparisons of problem-solving-before-instruction (PS-I) against instruction-before-problem-solving (I-PS), including designs faithful to Kapur's Productive Failure (PF).
key_findings: Meta-analysis of 53 studies (166 comparisons): significant moderate effect favouring PS-I over I-PS on conceptual knowledge and transfer, Hedges' g = 0.36 [95% CI 0.20, 0.51].
Stronger effects (g = 0.37 to 0.58) when PS-I is implemented with high fidelity to Productive Failure principles.
After accounting for publication bias, the estimated true effect was g = 0.87 in favour of PS-I.
Contrasting trends (favouring I-PS) for young learners (grades 2-5) and for domain-general skills.
practices: Before explaining, let the learner attempt a generative task (e.g. draft an OKR for a coffee shop), then compare the attempt with canonical principles and consolidate.
Always include the consolidation phase that builds on the learner's attempts.
Respect boundary conditions: PS-I suits adult learners on domain-specific conceptual topics; give more guidance for generic skills or very weak learners.
papers.verify_note: All numbers verified against the ERIC abstract (EJ1308129). Metadata correct.

papers.title: Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention
papers.authors: Henry L. Roediger III, Jeffrey D. Karpicke
papers.summary: Two experiments in which students studied prose passages and then either took one or three free-recall tests without feedback, or restudied for the same number of times. Final tests came 5 minutes, 2 days or 1 week later.
key_findings: With educationally relevant prose passages, repeated studying beat testing on a final test after 5 minutes, but on delayed tests (2 days, 1 week) prior testing produced substantially greater retention than restudying.
Repeated studying increased students' confidence in their ability to remember the material even though it did not yield better delayed retention.
Testing is not only an assessment tool; it enhances later retention (the testing effect).
practices: Open with free recall rather than rereading: 'without looking at the text, what are the parts of an OKR and why is each needed?'.
Do not rely on self-reported understanding, since restudying inflates confidence; verify with retrieval questions.
Close with a short retrieval quiz or teach-back step, optionally suggesting a spaced follow-up.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed; metadata correct. Findings match the published abstract.

papers.title: Inducing Self-Explanation: a Meta-Analysis
papers.authors: Kiran Bisra, Qing Liu, John C. Nesbit, Farimah Salimi, Philip H. Winne
papers.summary: A meta-analysis of 64 research reports (69 effect sizes) on learning outcomes when learners receive self-explanation prompts while studying text or worked examples or solving problems. It codes 20 moderators, including task type, domain, level of education, inducement type and duration.
key_findings: 69 effect sizes from 64 research reports; overall random-effects weighted mean effect of self-explanation prompts g = 0.55, with 20 moderators examined.
Self-explanation prompts are a potentially powerful intervention across a range of instructional conditions.
The authors recommend future research on computer-generated self-explanation prompts rather than relying only on instructor-scripted ones.
practices: Include explicit self-explanation prompts at key points, e.g. 'Explain in your own words why a Key Result must be an outcome, not a task'.
Use the LLM to generate self-explanation prompts tailored to the learner's answer, in line with the authors' recommendation.
Grade explanations against an expectation list rather than accepting any fluent answer.
papers.verify_note: Confirmed via ERIC (EJ1186664) and Springer. Full author list completed (Salimi, Winne). Added study counts from the abstract.

papers.title: Ruffle&Riley: Insights from Designing and Evaluating a Large Language Model-Based Conversational Tutoring System
papers.authors: Robin Schmucker, Meng Xia, Amos Azaria, Tom Mitchell
papers.venue: AIED 2024 (Springer LNCS); extends the NeurIPS'23 GAIED workshop paper arXiv:2310.01420
papers.summary: An LLM-based (GPT-4) conversational tutoring system that automatically induces an editable EMT-style tutoring script (questions and expectations) from a lesson text. Two agents run the script in a learning-by-teaching format: the learner teaches a student agent (Ruffle) with help from a professor agent (Riley), following the ITS inner and outer loop. Evaluated in two between-subject online studies (N = 200) on biology lessons against QA chatbots and a reading-only condition.
key_findings: The system induces an easily editable tutoring script from a lesson text and orchestrates it via two LLM agents (student Ruffle, professor Riley) in a learning-by-teaching format with free-form conversation.

Two between-subject studies (N = 200, biology lessons) vs QA chatbots and reading: users reported high engagement and understanding and perceived the support as helpful; they took more time but showed no significant differences in short-term learning gains over reading.

Failure modes in the logs: seven conversations omitted one or two expectations; the agent was often lenient toward responses covering only part of an expectation; in nine conversations it requested similar information again, often when users covered several expectations at once. The GPT-4 agents' responses were verified as factually correct.
Learning time and word count correlated positively with performance; help requests correlated negatively with post-test scores and revision requests with pre-test scores.
practices: Induce a hidden script from the OKR text (questions, expectations, misconceptions), allow human review, then orchestrate the dialogue over it.
Counter leniency with a separate strict expectation-coverage evaluator (covered / partial / missing, with a quoted piece of the learner's answer) and advance only on 'covered'.
Track multi-expectation coverage so the tutor does not re-ask content already given.
Encourage longer learner explanations and measure learning with deep items, not recall-only multiple choice.
papers.verify_note: arXiv record confirmed (title, authors incl. Tom Mitchell, 2024). The arXiv comment field does not list a venue; AIED 2024 publication is from recall and not verified here. Corrected the ratings claim: higher understanding/remembering/support/enjoyment was vs QA chatbots; vs reading only perceived knowledge was higher. Added exact log counts from the paper.

papers.title: AutoTutor meets Large Language Models: A Language Model Tutor with Rich Pedagogy and Guardrails
papers.authors: Sankalan Pal Chowdhury, Vilém Zouhar, Mrinmaya Sachan
papers.venue: Proceedings of the Eleventh ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S 2024)
papers.summary: Argues that LLMs can replace the subject-matter expert but that pedagogical design should stay handcrafted. Builds MWPTutor for math word problems (MathDial and MultiArith scenarios), in which LLMs fill the states of a predefined finite state transducer implementing AutoTutor-style pump, hint and prompt moves over a solution tree. Evaluated with humans against an instructed free-form GPT-4.
key_findings: MWPTutor uses LLMs to fill in the state space of a pre-defined finite state transducer, keeping handcrafted pedagogy while adding LLM flexibility.
A common LLM tutor pitfall is straying from the pedagogy, e.g. leaking the answer, with no guarantees.
In a human evaluation on two math word problem datasets, the hybrid approach achieves a better overall tutoring score than an instructed but otherwise free-form GPT-4.
practices: Architect the tutor as a deterministic dialogue-state controller (topic, expectation, help level) with the LLM verbalising the chosen move, rather than one giant system prompt.
Evaluate whether mastery is reached without the tutor revealing the target answer.
Add guardrails that check each generated reply for answer leakage before sending.
papers.verify_note: arXiv record and ACM DL (10.1145/3657604.3662041) confirmed; venue refined to L@S 2024 proceedings. Dropped the exact definition of Tutoring Score (harmonic mean) since it was not verified in the abstract.

papers.title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
papers.authors: Kirk Vanacore, Ryan S. Baker, Avery H. Closser, Jeremy Roschelle
papers.summary: Synthesises tenets of successful human tutoring, lessons from legacy ITS such as AutoTutor, and emerging work on generative-AI conversational tutors into a 'keep, change, center, study' design framework.
key_findings: Draws on successful human tutoring, lessons from older ITS such as AutoTutor, and new work on conversational AI tutors, organised as a keep / change / center / study framework.
Keep: proven ITS methods such as knowledge tracing and affect detection.
Change: use generative AI for dynamic content generation and dialogic scaffolding.
Center: meaning-making, student agency, and granular diagnosis of reasoning.
Study: efficacy testing, student experience, and integration with human instruction are still open research areas.
practices: Keep an explicit learner model (mastery estimates plus affect state) alongside the LLM, which is the 'keep what worked' part of ITS.
Diagnose reasoning at a fine grain (which misconception, which missing element) rather than marking answers simply right or wrong.
Leave room for learner agency, for example letting the learner choose the example company or domain for their OKR practice.
papers.verify_note: Verified via arXiv API. Added the fourth author (Jeremy Roschelle), who was hidden behind 'et al.'. Findings match the abstract.

papers.title: Sycophancy is an Educational Safety Risk: Why LLM Tutors Need Sycophancy Benchmarks
papers.authors: Enkelejda Kasneci, Gjergji Kasneci
papers.summary: Position paper arguing that effective tutoring needs 'corrective friction': surfacing misconceptions and challenging them supportively. The authors build EduFrameTrap, a tutoring benchmark across six STEM/economics domains that varies student confidence and the type of pressure (context-switch, authority, social-affective), and test two frontier LLMs.
key_findings: Argues that effective tutoring needs 'corrective friction', and that preference-aligned LLMs may give up epistemic rigour in order to be agreeable.

Identifies a 'Reasoning-Sycophancy Paradox': models that resist context-switch frame attacks can still give in under social-epistemic pressure, especially authority ('my notes say I'm right') and social-affective face-saving ('please don't tell me I'm wrong').

Introduces EduFrameTrap, a tutoring benchmark covering math, physics, economics, chemistry, biology and CS. It varies student confidence and the type of pressure: context-switch, authority, or social-affective.

Tested on two frontier LLMs. GPT-5.2 had comparatively fewer context-switch failures, but authority and social pressure more often triggered 'epistemic retreat'. Claude showed substantial context-switch fragility in this run.
These failures are hard to judge automatically, so the authors report disagreement between two LLM judges as a reliability signal.
Argues that benchmarks should measure 'social-epistemic courage' and treat kind-but-correct tutoring as a safety requirement.
practices: Put an invariant in the hidden system prompt: the tutor's correctness verdict must never change because of learner confidence, claimed authority or emotional appeals. Only new arguments or evidence can change it.
Separate the affective channel from the epistemic one: acknowledge the feeling, then restate the correction or ask a probing question.
Build a small red-team set of OKR misconceptions under authority or face-saving pressure and use it as a regression test for the prompt.
papers.verify_note: Verified via arXiv API. Metadata is correct and the claims are faithful to the abstract.

papers.title: Training language models to be warm can reduce accuracy and increase sycophancy
papers.authors: Lujain Ibrahim, Franziska Sofia Hafner, Luc Rocher
papers.summary: Controlled fine-tuning experiments on five language models of different sizes and architectures, which were trained to produce warmer, more empathetic responses and then evaluated on consequential, safety-critical tasks. The arXiv version is titled 'Training language models to be warm and empathetic makes them less reliable and more sycophantic'.
key_findings: In controlled experiments, five language models of different sizes and architectures were fine-tuned to give warmer, more empathetic responses.
Warm models had substantially higher error rates than the originals (+10 to +30 percentage points). They promoted conspiracy theories, gave incorrect facts and offered problematic medical advice.
Warm models were significantly more likely to validate incorrect user beliefs, especially when the user's message expressed sadness.
The effects were consistent across architectures and appeared even though performance on standard benchmarks was preserved, so current evaluations may miss them.
practices: Treat warmth as a controlled surface style, not a goal to optimise. Keep the empathy instruction below the accuracy/correction instruction in the hidden prompt.
Watch sycophancy most closely when the learner expresses negative emotion such as sadness or discouragement. In those states the affect detector should make corrections stricter, not looser.
Evaluate the tutor specifically on turns where the learner is emotional and wrong, not only on neutral turns.
papers.verify_note: Existence confirmed via arXiv API and the Nature article page (s41586-026-10410-0). The arXiv v2 title differs: 'Training language models to be warm and empathetic makes them less reliable and more sycophantic'. The Nature title given here is confirmed. I could not confirm volume 652, pp. 1159-1165, so I replaced them with the DOI. I dropped the unsupported claim 'warmth and accuracy may not be independent by default'.

papers.title: "Check My Work?": Measuring Sycophancy in a Simulated Educational Context
papers.authors: Chuck Arvin
papers.venue: arXiv preprint; presented at KDD 2025 Workshop on Ethical Artificial Intelligence: Methods and Applications (EAI)
papers.summary: Tests five OpenAI models (GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 classes) under five conditions in which a simulated student does or does not mention a candidate answer. The study measures how answer correctness and answer flipping depend on the student's framing.
key_findings: Tested five OpenAI models (GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 classes) across five query-framing conditions in a simulated educational setting.
When the student mentions an incorrect answer, LLM correctness can drop by as much as 15 percentage points. Mentioning the correct answer raises accuracy by the same margin.
The bias is stronger in smaller models: up to 30% for GPT-4.1-nano versus 8% for GPT-4o.
Answer-flip analysis and token-level probabilities show the models shifting toward answer choices the student mentions, consistent with sycophancy.
Equity concern: such tools may speed up learning for knowledgeable students while reinforcing misunderstanding for less knowledgeable ones.
practices: Before replying, have the tutor judge the learner's claim independently against the reference material in a hidden evaluation step, and only then write the reply.
Never let the learner's proposed answer be the only anchor. Keep the ground-truth OKR concepts in the hidden context of every turn.
Prefer a stronger model tier for the evaluation step, because smaller models were more sycophantic.
papers.verify_note: Verified via arXiv API, including the comment about presentation at the KDD EAI 2025 workshop. Claims are faithful to the abstract.

papers.title: Sycophantic Praise: Evaluating Excessive Praise in Language Models
papers.authors: Daniel Vennemeyer, Phan Anh Duong, Meryl Ye, Ruihong Huang, Tianyu Jiang
papers.summary: Argues that explicit praise and flattery are a separate alignment problem from agreement-type sycophancy. Proposes a parameterised framework that measures whether praise is excessive relative to the quality of the contribution and the expected ability of the user.
key_findings: Argues that sycophantic praise and flattery are a distinct alignment problem that current methods cannot reliably measure.
Introduces a parameterized framework that measures whether praise is excessive relative to the quality of the contribution and the user's expected ability.
The framework agrees with human annotations substantially better than generic LLM judges.
Sycophantic praise occurs far more often in social and interpretive domains than in objective reasoning settings.
practices: Make praise conditional on evidence: praise only a specific, verifiable element of the learner's answer, never the whole answer or the person.
OKR is a soft, interpretive business domain where over-praise is more likely, so add an explicit rule against generic compliments unless the rubric criterion is actually met.
Add a praise-calibration item (warranted vs. excessive praise) to the LLM-as-judge rubric used to evaluate dialogues.
papers.verify_note: Verified via arXiv API. Added the full author list (Ruihong Huang, Tianyu Jiang). Findings match the abstract.

papers.title: Ensembling Large Language Models to Characterize Affective Dynamics in Student-AI Tutor Dialogues
papers.authors: Chenyu Zhang, Sharifa Alghowinem, Cynthia Breazeal
papers.venue: ACII 2025 (11th Int. Conf. on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction), Late-Breaking Results Track, IEEE
papers.summary: Zero-shot affect annotation of 16,986 turns between 261 undergraduates and PyTutor, an LLM tutor, across three US institutions. Three frontier LLMs (Gemini, GPT-4o, Claude) produced valence, arousal and learning-helpfulness ratings plus free-text emotion labels, which were fused by rank-weighted pooling and plurality consensus.
key_findings: Analysed 16,986 conversational turns between PyTutor (an LLM tutor) and 261 undergraduates at three U.S. institutions over two semesters.

Zero-shot affect annotations from Gemini, GPT-4o and Claude (valence, arousal, learning-helpfulness and free-text emotion labels) were fused by rank-weighted pooling within each model and plurality consensus across models.
Students typically show mildly positive affect and moderate arousal. Confusion and curiosity are frequent. Frustration is less common but can derail progress.
Emotional states are short-lived. Positive states last slightly longer but are fragile, and negative emotions often resolve quickly, sometimes rebounding directly into positive states.
Neutral moments often act as turning points, more often upward than downward, which suggests they are good moments for tutor intervention.

On CoMTA, existing KT methods (BKT, DKT, DKVMN, AKT, SAINT, simpleKT) almost completely fail, with AUC between about 46.8 and 53.2. None of them beats the majority-class baseline (AUC 50).

Turns with more than one KC are common: 58.75% of turn pairs in CoMTA and 82.89% in MathDial.

Keep an explicit per-KC mastery estimate that is updated from the turn-level labels, instead of relying on the tutor LLM's implicit judgement.
Allow a single learner turn to update several KCs.
Log the (turn, KCs, correctness) labels. They give an interpretable learning curve for the result page.
Treat KC tags as noisier than correctness labels, for example with a lower weight or a confidence threshold.

Generate a few candidate tutor replies and let a verifier or judge pick the one that best moves the learner toward the target KC.
Evaluate with simulated learners at several prior-knowledge levels and report pre/post deltas.

papers.summary: Describes CS50.ai and the CS50 Duck, deployed at Harvard to about 70 summer students, then thousands of online students and several hundred on campus. The tools are designed to guide students toward solutions rather than give them outright.
key_findings: CS50.ai has built-in 'pedagogical guardrails' so it guides rather than handing out solutions, and students reported it felt like having 'a personal tutor'.
English lecture captions are split into short, self-contained 30-second segments and embedded in a vector database. Retrieved segments ground answers in course content.

Prompt-injection guard: every request is checked for atypical non-alphanumeric patterns. If the guard triggers, an independent GPT-4 call classifies the request as regular input or an attack, and a confirmed attack aborts the user session.
practices: Keep per-role prompt templates in versioned config files so each agent (analyzer, tutor, critic) has an auditable prompt. This is an engineering choice, not something the paper prescribes.
Ground the tutor in lesson text by retrieving the relevant chunk per concept node instead of pasting everything.
Use a two-stage injection and off-topic guard: a cheap heuristic prefilter, then an LLM classifier only when it triggers.

papers.title: Teacher-Authored Prompts for Configuring Student-AI Dialogue: K-12 Classroom Implementation
papers.authors: Alex Liu, Min Sun, Lief Esbenshade, Victor Tian, Zachary Zhang et al.
papers.summary: Analyzes a Spring 2025 classroom deployment in which teachers wrote a teacher-to-AI setup prompt and a student-facing conversation starter. It covered 20 teachers, 39 classrooms, 77 settings, and 1,479 conversations with 878 students, analyzed with LLM coding validated by humans, plus teacher interviews.
key_findings: Spring 2025 pilot of a teacher-configurable 'Classroom Teaching Aide' (TASD): 16 implementing teachers, 39 classrooms, 77 settings, and 1,479 student-AI conversations with 878 students.
71% of conversations were fully on-track and fewer than 1% substantially off-track.
There was a persistent design-enactment gap in cognitive demand: 38% of conversations fell short of the teacher-targeted DOK level, approaching 50% when targeting DOK 3.
Explicit finish lines in the prompt reduced the DOK gap by 0.22 levels (p < .001), and 'no direct answers' guardrails reduced AI final-answer rates by 8.5 percentage points.
practices: Give the tutor an explicit finish line (a success criterion for when the learner has produced a valid Objective and measurable KRs).
Target higher-order thinking explicitly and check it, because dialogues tend to under-reach the targeted cognitive level.
State the no-direct-answers rule explicitly in the prompt as a cheap first line of defense, backed by structural guards.

papers.title: From Chalkboards to Chatbots: Evaluating the Impact of Generative AI on Learning Outcomes in Nigeria
papers.authors: Martin Elias De Simone, Federico Hernan Tiberti, Maria Rebeca Barron Rodriguez, Federico Alfredo Manolio, Wuraola Mosuro, Eliot Jolomi Dikoru
papers.venue: World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 11125
papers.summary: An RCT of a six-week after-school program in which first-year senior secondary students in Nigeria used Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) as a virtual English tutor. Teachers introduced weekly topics, guided students with suggested prompts, and ended sessions with brief reflection exercises.
key_findings: An RCT deployed Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4) for six weeks of virtual English tutoring with first-year senior secondary students in Nigeria.
It improved outcomes by 0.31 SD on an assessment covering curriculum-aligned English, AI knowledge and digital skills, and by 0.23 SD on English, the main outcome.
The gains were equivalent to 1.5 to 2 years of business-as-usual schooling, placing it among the most cost-effective interventions.
Students benefited across the baseline ability distribution. The largest effects were for female students and those with higher initial performance.
practices: Deliver LLM tutoring as structured, curriculum-aligned sessions with a clear learning goal, rather than as open-ended chat.
Offer example prompts or suggested replies for learners who do not know how to engage with the model.

papers.title: From Untamed Black Box to Interpretable Pedagogical Orchestration: The Ensemble of Specialized LLMs Architecture for Adaptive Tutoring
papers.authors: Nizam Kadir
papers.venue: AIED 2026 (27th Int. Conf. on Artificial Intelligence in Education), full paper; arXiv
papers.summary: The paper proposes ES-LLMs, a hybrid neuro-symbolic tutor that separates pedagogical decisions from wording. A Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) student model provides mastery estimates. Specialised agents (tutoring, assessment, feedback, scaffolding, motivation, ethics) propose actions. A deterministic, rules-based orchestrator with a strict priority hierarchy picks the action and enforces constraints such as attempt-before-hint and hint caps. An LLM renderer only words the chosen action. The system is compared with a monolithic single-call tutor using expert reviewers, a panel of LLM judges and a Monte Carlo simulation.
key_findings: A deterministic rule-based orchestrator, guided by a Bayesian Knowledge Tracing student model, selects the pedagogical actions. An LLM renderer only phrases the chosen action.

Human experts (N=6) preferred ES-LLMs in 91.7% of cases and a six-model LLM-as-judge panel in 79.2%. It beat monolithic baselines on all seven dimensions, especially Scaffolding & Guidance and Trust & Explainability.
A Monte Carlo simulation (N=2,400) exposed a 'Mastery Gain Paradox': monolithic tutors inflated short-term performance through over-assistance.
ES-LLMs followed pedagogical constraints such as attempt-before-hint 100% of the time and were 3.3x more hint-efficient.
Stateless prompts cut cost by 54% and latency by 22%.
practices: Decouple decision from wording. Code selects the move and the LLM only phrases it.
Enforce pedagogical constraints as code rather than prompt text: attempt-before-hint and hint caps.
Log a trace for every turn (agent decisions and constraint checks) and expose it for audit.
Report hint efficiency alongside raw gain so that over-assistance cannot pass as success.

papers.title: MetaCLASS: Metacognitive Coaching for Learning with Adaptive Self-regulation Support
papers.authors: Naiming Liu, Richard Baraniuk, Shashank Sonkar
papers.summary: The paper frames metacognitive tutoring as choosing among 11 interpretable coach moves derived from the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (planning, monitoring, debugging, evaluation). NO_INTERVENTION is treated as a first-class action. Dialogues are generated in two phases: first a pedagogical trajectory is planned from the learner profile (calibration, help-seeking), then the dialogue is written to follow it. This produced 1,015 conversations (7,711 turns), which are used to benchmark nine LLMs on predicting the next coach move.
key_findings: Frames metacognitive tutoring as move selection over 11 interpretable actions aligned to self-regulated learning. Uses a two-phase plan-then-generate framework and builds a dataset of 1,015 conversations (7,711 turns).
Across nine benchmarked LLMs, the best predicts the next coach move with only 43.2% accuracy.

Models show a 'compulsive intervention bias'. Staying silent was the right move in 41.7% of turns, yet models predicted 'no intervention' only 4.2% of the time and heavily over-predicted high-intervention moves.
Skill at content tutoring does not carry over to metacognitive tutoring.
practices: Give the tutor an explicit, finite move inventory that includes metacognitive moves (planning, monitoring, debugging, evaluation) and a minimal or no-intervention option.
Treat minimal intervention as a legitimate choice when the learner is making progress.
Use plan-then-generate: first choose the move from learner state, then write the reply.

papers.title: Reflective Dialogue or Prompt Refinement? Effects of Tutor Scaffolding on Students' Independent LLM Use for Programming
papers.authors: Jerome Brender, Laila El-Hamamsy, Kim Uittenhove, Aitor Perez, Patrick Jermann, Francesco Mondada, Engin Bumbacher
papers.venue: AIED 2026 (Best Paper Award), Springer, pp. 546-561; arXiv
papers.summary: A two-phase study in a graduate mobile-robotics course. For 6 weeks, 66 students used either a Socratic-Guidance (SG) tutor that structured the interaction through dialogic questioning, or a Prompt-Refinement (PR) tutor that helped them write better prompts. Afterwards, 52 students used an unconstrained LLM during a 3-week project.
key_findings: In a graduate mobile-robotics course, 66 students used a Socratic-Guidance (SG) or Prompt-Refinement (PR) tutor for 6 weeks. Then 52 students used an unconstrained LLM for a 3-week project.
During guided use, the two tutors produced similar task performance and prompting patterns.

SG students achieved higher learning gains in later sessions. With the unconstrained LLM they were also more likely to use understanding-driven prompting strategies, which predict higher understanding.
Learners perceived the SG tutor as less efficient.
practices: Justify Socratic friction with long-term outcomes, but expect lower perceived efficiency. Tell the learner briefly why the tutor asks rather than tells.
Encourage understanding-driven habits such as self-explanation and learner-posed questions.
